# Network research orchestrator report

Research date: 2026-10-11.

## 1. Result

The evidence supports a layered, measured `bench network` design.
Start with topology and actual transport selection.
Then test isolated rails, directions, concurrent rails, and representative endpoint pairs.
Run operation-specific NCCL sweeps and save raw results.
Check counter changes, rank/host timing, cleanup, and a fresh post-test canary.
The research does not certify the Chennai rack.
No researcher runs live fabric tests.

Target: GB300 NVL72-class, 18 trays, Chennai, India.
Scope: east-west fabric only.
Excluded: north-south internet, storage, code changes, and live certification.

Exactly seven researchers supply the original seven independent category nodes.
Eleven additional researchers supply the O'Reilly source supplement.
All use `agent=researcher` and `model=openai-codex/gpt-6-luna`.
The children change only their briefs and start no agents.
The orchestrator writes only inside `.lavish/network-research/`.

# Academic methods for diagnosing east-west fabric quality

Research date: 2026-10-11. All claims below carry a source URL.

Claims are tagged **[observed]** (directly supported by a cited source), **[calculated]** (arithmetic from cited definitions), or **[inference]** (recommended interpretation/design). Scope is only N06 / academia: academic methods and primary technical sources for diagnosing congestion and collective limits in an 18-tray GB300-class rack within a two-hour network certification window. This is not a claim that all suggested tests already exist in rack-bench.

## 1. What the measurement must answer

A collective benchmark alone says that an operation took a given time; it does not identify whether the limiting resource was GPU/NVLink, PCIe/C2C, NIC, one rail, a switch path, congestion, CPU progress, or the collective algorithm. NVIDIA explicitly says NCCL `busbw` estimates the bottleneck hardware bandwidth and may correspond to NVLink, PCI, QPI, or network—not necessarily the external fabric. [observed] [NCCL performance definitions](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests/blob/master/doc/PERFORMANCE.md)

**[inference]** A defensible certificate therefore pairs (1) collective scaling measurements with (2) one-rail and concurrent-rail RDMA measurements, (3) rail/topology isolation, and (4) before/after counter deltas. Correlation among those independent views is the diagnosis; no single peak number establishes fabric health.

The local design context targets an 18-tray NVL72-class rack; it calls for an 8 B–16 GB NCCL sweep, `algbw`/`busbw`, perftest and a multi-node collective, while recognizing a monotonicity heuristic. [observed] [README.md](../../README.md#L320-L348) It also calls out per-rail QP sanity, a two-rank all-reduce canary, expected rail naming, and NCCL configuration as active bench checks. [observed] [README.md](../../README.md#L220-L240) These local excerpts are context, not independent evidence for performance claims.

## 2. NCCL bandwidth definitions: use the right numerator

Let **S** be the operation's total logical payload in bytes, **t** the measured operation time in seconds, and **n** participating ranks. NCCL-tests defines algorithm bandwidth as `algbw = S/t` (GB/s in output). It is a useful application-level throughput, but its peak depends on collective and rank count. [observed] [NCCL-tests performance document](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests/blob/master/doc/PERFORMANCE.md)

For point-to-point Send/Recv and root-centric Broadcast/Reduce, the documented correction factor is 1: `busbw = algbw`. For AllReduce, `busbw = algbw × 2(n−1)/n`; for ReduceScatter and AllGather, `busbw = algbw × (n−1)/n`; AlltoAll also uses `(n−1)/n`. [observed] [NCCL-tests performance document](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests/blob/master/doc/PERFORMANCE.md)

**Why AllReduce's factor:** each element needs `n−1` additions and distribution to all ranks; under the document's point-to-point model this is `2(n−1)` transfers shared over `n` ranks/links. Ideal time is `t = (S/B) × 2(n−1)/n`, hence `B = (S/t) × 2(n−1)/n`. ReduceScatter performs only the reduction traffic; AllGather only distribution traffic, so each factor is `(n−1)/n`. [observed] [NCCL-tests performance document](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests/blob/master/doc/PERFORMANCE.md)

**[calculated] Example, 8 ranks:** AllReduce factor = 14/8 = 1.75; if `algbw=100 GB/s`, `busbw=175 GB/s`. ReduceScatter or AllGather factor = 7/8 = 0.875, giving 87.5 GB/s. Those values are normalization, not physical wire counters. Comparing `busbw` to one NIC's line rate is invalid if it includes faster intra-tray links or concurrent rails; compare only to a stated topology-aware bottleneck budget. [inference] [NCCL-tests definition](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests/blob/master/doc/PERFORMANCE.md); [Nebius NCCL test interpretation](https://docs.nebius.com/slurm-soperator/jobs/examples/nccl-all-reduce)

NCCL's document defines **S as total array bytes** for ReduceScatter and AllGather: per-rank `recvcount × datatype_size × n` and `sendcount × datatype_size × n`, respectively. [observed] [NCCL-tests performance document](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests/blob/master/doc/PERFORMANCE.md) **[inference]** Store the command, rank count, datatype, per-rank count, total S, time, algorithm/protocol selection, and both bandwidth columns with every result; otherwise independently recomputing `algbw` can silently use the wrong S.

## 3. Collective limits: separate algorithm, topology, and congestion

Ring AllReduce is bandwidth-efficient for large messages: it decomposes into reduce-scatter plus all-gather. Across both phases, each rank sends a total of `2S(n−1)/n` bytes and receives the same volume for an S-byte tensor—not `2S(n−1)/n` in each phase. [observed] [NCCL-tests performance document](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests/blob/master/doc/PERFORMANCE.md); [Patarasuk & Yuan, bandwidth-optimal AllReduce](https://www.cs.fsu.edu/~xyuan/paper/07hips.pdf) Tree methods reduce dependency depth for small-message latency but change path pressure and can expose root/branch bottlenecks. NCCL's primary test documentation explicitly says its bus-bandwidth accounting is independent of point-to-point algorithm choice under its transfer model; real hardware's selected algorithm/protocol and topology can still change measured time. [observed] [NCCL-tests performance document](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests/blob/master/doc/PERFORMANCE.md); [NCCL technical report, Jeaugey, OLCF PDF](https://www.olcf.ornl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/Summit-NCCL.pdf)

The NCCL technical report documents Tree and Ring AllReduce as distinct algorithms, describing Tree as log-latency and Ring as linear-latency with high bandwidth. [observed] [NCCL technical report](https://www.olcf.ornl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/Summit-NCCL.pdf) **[inference]** Evaluate both latency-sensitive small payloads and throughput-sensitive large payloads through normal auto-selection; if the library supports a controlled diagnostic override, compare algorithm/protocol variants as a *triage experiment*, not as the acceptance default. Forcing an algorithm can create a non-production path.

AlltoAll is a useful complement to AllReduce: every rank exchanges distinct data, so its traffic pattern and hotspot behavior are not captured by a ring AllReduce. NVIDIA describes all-to-all as prone to congestion/hotspots at scale and discusses routing/message aggregation optimizations. [observed] [NVIDIA NCCL all-to-all technical article](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/doubling-all2all-performance-with-nvidia-collective-communication-library-2-12) **[inference]** In a short rack test, use an AlltoAll point at representative small/medium sizes (or a short sweep) to expose path entropy and incast/contention problems, but do not interpret it as a universal training workload.

### Halving-doubling / Rabenseifner tradeoff

Rabenseifner-style AllReduce combines reduce-scatter with allgather, commonly using recursive halving then recursive doubling for power-of-two rank counts. The method reaches the bandwidth communication-volume lower bound while using logarithmic communication rounds, unlike a simple ring's linear round count. Large payloads can benefit from the lower round count and volume; small payloads are dominated by per-round latency and startup. Non-power-of-two rank counts require variants and can add imbalance or communication. [observed] [Rabenseifner, “Optimization of Collective Reduction Operations”](https://www.hlrs.de/people/rabenseifner/papers); [Patarasuk & Yuan, bandwidth-optimal AllReduce](https://www.cs.fsu.edu/~xyuan/paper/07hips.pdf)

The tradeoff is topology-sensitive: recursive partner exchanges may load specific cuts or map poorly to multi-rail and hierarchical GPU fabrics, while a ring can pipeline evenly when its logical ring matches physical links. Neither is universally superior. [inference] [NCCL technical report](https://www.olcf.ornl.gov/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/Summit-NCCL.pdf); [Patarasuk & Yuan](https://www.cs.fsu.edu/~xyuan/paper/07hips.pdf) **[inference]** Observe the normal library-selected algorithm; use forced variants only as controlled diagnostics, not acceptance defaults.

### Message-size sweeps and protocol switching

For each collective, span 8 B to 16 GB with logarithmic/geometric sizes, repeat selected points, and retain raw time as well as `algbw` and `busbw`. Small messages primarily reveal fixed launch/communication latency; large messages increasingly reveal throughput. [observed] [NCCL-tests performance document](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests/blob/master/doc/PERFORMANCE.md)

**Strict monotonicity is unsafe.** NCCL's algorithm and protocol choices may change across payload sizes; tiny-message latency, chunking, pipeline depth, channel count, registration, and hardware tiers also alter the curve. A switch in regime may create a legitimate step or local dip, while a bad link can still produce a smooth but low curve. **[inference]** Treat curve discontinuities as investigation signals, not automatic failure; classify against repeated-run noise and matched algorithm/protocol metadata. Never require every successive `busbw` point to increase. The NCCL performance source explains the latency-to-bandwidth regime transition, but does not promise monotonicity. [observed] [NCCL-tests performance document](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests/blob/master/doc/PERFORMANCE.md)

### Concurrent rail aggregation

Measure each rail alone, then all expected rails concurrently with traffic bound to their intended devices. **[inference]** Compare aggregate goodput to the sum of isolated-rail goodputs and to the topology's realizable egress/ingress budget; also preserve per-rail results. If each rail is healthy alone but aggregate does not scale, suspect shared switch uplinks, bad rail placement/routing, NIC/PCIe/GPU feed limits, CPU launch/affinity, or congestion—not simply a slow port. If one rail alone is weak and its pinned collective degrades similarly, the fault is localized more strongly.

A collective may send intra-node data on NVLink and cross-node data on RDMA, so a high normalized `busbw` does not prove the NIC sustained that rate. Nebius explicitly cautions that two-node mixed NVLink/InfiniBand AllReduce can make `busbw` overestimate InfiniBand load. [observed] [Nebius NCCL test interpretation](https://docs.nebius.com/slurm-soperator/jobs/examples/nccl-all-reduce) **[inference]** Pin ranks and NIC rails, record NCCL topology/debug logs, and use concurrent per-rail RDMA as the external-fabric cross-check.

## 4. Controlled checks within two hours

The following is an evidence-oriented time budget, not a vendor-independent pass threshold. **[inference]** Run independent per-rail tasks in parallel only if the test harness can bind them and capture counters without competing with the collective phase.

| Approx. window | Check | Diagnostic value |
|---|---|---|
| 0–10 min | Snapshot NIC/switch counters; verify active rate, link layer, expected rail map, errors; per-rail QP/connectivity sanity. | Excludes obvious downshift, missing rail, bad route/configuration before interpreting bandwidth. [NVIDIA troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html) |
| 10–35 min | Per-rail RDMA write and read bandwidth over several sizes; small-message latency; host-memory and GPU-memory path where supported. | Direct link/path evidence; direction and host/GPU-path comparison. [NVIDIA troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html) |
| 35–80 min | NCCL AllReduce/AllGather/AlltoAll geometric 8 B–16 GB sweep; multiple ranks and MPI plus torch.distributed launch path; repeat boundary/representative points. | Exposes collective scaling, wrong transport, threshold/protocol changes, rank/launch issues. [NCCL-tests](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests/blob/master/doc/PERFORMANCE.md) |
| 80–105 min | Concurrent all-rail bandwidth, then short concurrent collective + rail traffic if safe; snapshot counters. | Identifies aggregate oversubscription and contention sensitivity, not just isolated peak. [DCQCN paper](https://conferences.sigcomm.org/sigcomm/2015/pdf/papers/p523.pdf) |
| 105–120 min | Repeat anomalous points; correlate NCCL logs, per-rail performance, switch/NIC counter deltas; report uncertainty and unresolved causes. | Prevents a single transient or host stall becoming a false pass/fail. [NVIDIA troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html) |

An 18-tray rack has many links and rank placements. **[inference]** A two-hour bench cannot exhaustively test every ordered endpoint pair, all rail combinations, all message sizes repeatedly, or sustained thermal/failure behavior. Use topology-stratified pairs (same tray, neighboring trays, distinct switch/plane where known), all-rail aggregate, and explicit representative rankfiles; defer exhaustive mesh and long-duration stability to smoke.

## 5. Congestion causality: ECN, DCQCN, PFC, counters

DCQCN is an end-to-end, rate-based congestion-control design for RoCEv2. Its paper describes the path: switch ECN marks signal queue buildup; receiver notification (CNP) informs sender; sender reduces rate. PFC remains a loss-prevention backstop, not evidence that congestion is absent. The authors report improved throughput/fairness in a three-tier testbed, while explaining PFC can spread congestion. [observed] [Zhu et al., “Congestion Control for Large-Scale RDMA Deployments,” SIGCOMM 2015](https://conferences.sigcomm.org/sigcomm/2015/pdf/papers/p523.pdf)

ECN marks indicate that configured queue-marking conditions were met; they are not packet drops. A mark/CNP increase under load with stable throughput may indicate functioning congestion control. A mark increase plus queue/latency growth and throughput collapse suggests overload or ineffective control. Absence of visible marks does **not** prove no congestion: thresholds may be high, counters may not be exposed, or the bottleneck may be elsewhere. **[inference]** Report mark and CNP deltas with their device, priority/traffic class, time interval and counter source.

PFC pause counters show link-level pause activity, not flow-level attribution. PFC pauses act per port/priority, so unrelated flows sharing that class/path may stall: the DCQCN paper demonstrates unfairness and “victim flow” effects due to cascading pause propagation and head-of-line blocking. [observed] [DCQCN paper](https://conferences.sigcomm.org/sigcomm/2015/pdf/papers/p523.pdf) **[inference]** A pause delta with latency spikes or uneven pair throughput is a congestion warning, not necessarily a defective cable. Sustained pause storms or pause increases on unrelated links justify escalation to switch queue/route analysis.

Counters are implementation-specific and often split across NIC, switch, firmware, and driver. NVIDIA's troubleshooting guide recommends observing RoCE port errors, drops, pause/PFC counters and available ECN/CNP/queue-drop counters; it also names RDMA retry/sequence/timeout indicators and InfiniBand symbol, link-recovery, and link-down counters. [observed] [NVIDIA NCCL network troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html) **[inference]** Snapshot before/after and calculate deltas; cumulative nonzero counters can predate the run. Never label “ECN zero” or “PFC zero” as established unless the relevant counter is actually exposed and validated. Counter units and reset/wrap semantics must be recorded.

### InfiniBand congestion/performance evidence

Gran et al. experimentally studied InfiniBand hardware congestion control and reported that it can resolve congestion and improve fairness, including the parking-lot problem, when configured appropriately. This is an actual IB performance study, not a modern GB300 comparison; it shows why contention and fairness tests can reveal problems missed by unloaded peak bandwidth. [observed] [Gran et al., “First Experiences with Congestion Control in InfiniBand Hardware,” IPDPS 2010](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/5470419)

**[inference]** Add brief controlled contention (multiple senders sharing a receiver/path, with an unrelated victim flow if safely constructible) and compare per-flow goodput and latency with isolated baselines. Treat fairness as diagnostic evidence, not a universal threshold. Do not transplant the paper’s testbed results numerically to GB300.

### Failure and route diagnosis

NVIDIA recommends `ibstat`/`ibstatus` for active state, link layer and rate; `ib_write_bw`/`ib_write_lat` for direct bandwidth/latency; `rdma statistic` for retry/loss symptoms; `perfquery` for InfiniBand physical/link errors; and `ibdiagnet` for topology/routing diagnostics when switch-management access exists. It advises using GPU-memory variants to compare the GPUDirect path with host-memory results. [observed] [NVIDIA NCCL network troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)

**[inference]** To test failure causality safely, do not inject a physical failure during acceptance unless explicitly authorized. Instead detect naturally missing/downshifted links, compare each rail isolated and in aggregate, and correlate the bad rail with selected collective rankfiles and topology. An observed impairment under one rail plus corresponding link/recovery counters supports causality; a collective slowdown alone does not. Fabric-wide route/port diagnostics may require switch/Subnet Manager access unavailable to tenant-side tooling; record that as an evidence limitation, not a pass.

### Link failure and mitigation evidence

NetPilot’s primary SIGCOMM paper studies production datacenter failures and link-down mitigation. It shows how a failed member link can leave a logical LAG overloaded after traffic redistribution, and evaluates mitigation by estimating impact on maximum link utilization and packet loss before deactivation. Its scope is Ethernet scale-out datacenters, not GPU collectives or InfiniBand; the diagnostic lesson is to correlate link state, utilization imbalance and traffic impact rather than attribute a collective slowdown to a root cause by itself. [observed] [Wu et al., “NetPilot: Automating Datacenter Network Failure Mitigation,” SIGCOMM 2012](https://users.cs.duke.edu/~xwy/publications/2012_sigcomm_netpilot.pdf); [Microsoft Research](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/netpilot-automating-datacenter-network-failure-mitigation)

**[inference]** Use passive evidence in rack certification: expected versus active link count/rate, per-rail throughput, utilization and error/recovery counter deltas, correlated with rank placement. Do not inject or deactivate links routinely; fault injection requires authorization and redundancy headroom.

## 6. Read/write asymmetry and host confounds

RDMA write and read are not interchangeable probes. The DCQCN paper's early RoCE evaluation uses an RDMA **READ** workload and notes that operation semantics and sender/receiver roles differ; it also describes READ's loss-detection limitations in the implementation discussed. [observed] [DCQCN paper](https://conferences.sigcomm.org/sigcomm/2015/pdf/papers/p523.pdf) A read/write gap can arise from NIC protocol/firmware behavior, receiver-side processing, direction-specific path/congestion, PCIe/GPU data path, or benchmark setup—not necessarily asymmetric physical link capacity. [inference]

**[inference]** Run both directions with matched message sizes, QP count, MTU, duration, CPU affinity, memory registration and endpoint pair; repeat with endpoints swapped. Compare host-memory RDMA first, then GPU-memory/GDR path. If host-memory is symmetric but GPU-memory is not, suspect GPU/NIC locality, DMA-BUF/GDR support, PCIe/C2C or GPU feed. If both are asymmetric and the deficit follows a rail/route, fabric or NIC port is more likely. NVIDIA recommends host-vs-GPU-memory comparison for GPUDirect troubleshooting. [observed] [NVIDIA troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)

Host confounds include CPU scheduling/affinity, NUMA placement, PCIe congestion, GPU clocks/power/thermal state, insufficient pinned memory, QP creation/registration overhead, MPI progress/rendezvous, competing workloads and kernel/driver differences. NCCL documents pinned-memory registration failures as a cause of communication setup errors; NVIDIA's troubleshooting flow separates NIC, RDMA, and GPU-memory tests. [observed] [NVIDIA troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html) **[inference]** Capture GPU/NIC/NUMA affinity, clocks, CPU utilization, driver/NCCL versions, test command, rank mapping, and competing load to prevent host bottlenecks being misreported as fabric failure.

## 7. Statistical limits and pass/fail discipline

A two-hour sweep has finite samples and may miss rare congestion, intermittent link faults, burst-loss episodes, or thermal drift. NCCL output commonly aggregates iterations; means can hide tails. A single maximum-throughput result is not a stable estimate. [inference]

**[inference]** At minimum, repeat selected latency and throughput points enough to report median and spread (e.g., interquartile range or p95 where iteration samples exist); distinguish between-run variability from within-run tails. Do not present a p99 from a handful of samples as meaningful. Use warm-up and timed iterations, preserve raw logs, and state sample count and duration. Where only aggregate NCCL timing is available, label it as such rather than claiming a latency distribution.

No universal “percent of line rate” threshold follows from these academic sources. NCCL `busbw` is a model-based normalization and a topology may combine multiple link tiers; DCQCN results are workload/testbed-specific. [observed] [NCCL-tests](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests/blob/master/doc/PERFORMANCE.md); [DCQCN paper](https://conferences.sigcomm.org/sigcomm/2015/pdf/papers/p523.pdf) **[inference]** Set thresholds from the certified rack topology and known-good measured baseline, stratify by message regime and rail count, and attach uncertainty. Do not turn a marketing/vendor figure or a single academic testbed's result into a universal pass bar.

## 8. Actionable suite findings

1. **[inference] Normalize correctly.** Preserve total logical payload and apply collective-specific NCCL `busbw` factors; do not equate `busbw` with one external rail.
2. **[inference] Cross-check collective against point-to-point.** Per-rail RDMA plus all-rail aggregate localizes link/rail limits; NCCL reveals actual collective mapping and scale behavior.
3. **[inference] Replace strict monotonicity with regime-aware anomaly detection.** Protocol/algorithm transitions, small-message latency and tier changes can legitimately break monotonic curves; use repeatability and metadata.
4. **[inference] Measure congestion causally.** Pair throughput/latency anomalies with ECN/CNP, PFC, drops/retries, queue and physical-link counter deltas. ECN marks are not drops; PFC can cause head-of-line blocking even without packet loss.
5. **[inference] Separate device path from fabric.** Matched read/write, endpoint swap, host-vs-GPU memory and locality controls help distinguish asymmetry from host/GPU feed limits.
6. **[inference] Treat failure evidence conservatively.** A failing collective is symptom evidence; rail isolation plus link/route/counter correlation is stronger causal evidence. Do not actively pull links in an ordinary acceptance window.
7. **[inference] State what the window cannot prove.** Two hours can find gross, repeatable bottlenecks and concurrent-load contention; it cannot prove rare-event reliability, long-term congestion behavior or exhaustive pairwise correctness.

## Gaps

- **GB300-specific academic baseline:** no primary peer-reviewed source found in this research that establishes expected NCCL or per-rail values for a specific GB300 NVL72 18-tray rack. Thresholds must come from topology-aware local measurements and the accepted configuration.
- **Rail topology details:** README context indicates multiple rails, but this research did not independently verify the exact switch/rail wiring or oversubscription; aggregate capacity cannot be computed without that map.
- **Counter availability:** actual switch ASIC/firmware and tenant permissions are unknown. ECN marks, CNPs, PFC pause duration, queue occupancy, drops and route counters may not all be exposed; no visibility must be reported as a diagnostic gap.
- **NCCL algorithm/protocol metadata:** the primary performance document defines normalization, not a universal expected curve or all version-specific algorithm/protocol switching points. These vary with NCCL build, topology and hardware.
- **Academic RoCE-versus-IB comparability:** no matched contemporary GB300 study was obtained that controls identical GPU, NIC count, topology, congestion tuning and workload. Fabric-technology rankings should not be inferred from unpaired vendor figures.
- **Failure injection:** the two-hour acceptance recommendation is observational and safe by default. Controlled link/switch failure testing needs explicit operational approval and a separate fault-injection plan.
- **Search limitation:** additional searches were rate-limited; this brief consequently favors the fetched primary NCCL, SIGCOMM DCQCN and NVIDIA troubleshooting sources over weaker comparisons. No unsupported universal threshold is supplied.
ai-labs.md:
# AI-lab methods for diagnosing east-west fabric quality

Research date: 2026-10-11. All claims below carry a source URL.

## 1. Executive finding

AI labs diagnose fabric faults by correlating three kinds of evidence: (1) topology-aware collective performance across representative sizes/patterns, (2) rank-level timing that separates compute-ready time from communication/wait time, and (3) physical network/NIC/switch telemetry. A slow all-reduce alone does not prove a bad link: late data-loader batches, CPU proxy starvation, GPU throttling, workload imbalance, and communication itself can all make a rank arrive late. The strongest short certification therefore combines rank-matrix collectives with per-rail isolation and counter snapshots; sustained mixed-load fault discovery belongs in smoke/burn-in. **[inference]** [Meta SIGCOMM paper](https://cs.stanford.edu/~keithw/sigcomm2024/sigcomm24-final246-acmpaginated.pdf) [PyTorch DDP straggler analysis](https://pytorch.org/blog/straggler-mitigation) [Google Cloud straggler detection](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/compute/stragglers-in-ai-a-guide-to-automated-straggler-detection)

## 2. Production topology evidence: do not conflate designs

### 2.1 Meta: dedicated backend RoCE; topology and routing evolved by deployment

Meta describes separate frontend (data ingestion/checkpoint/logging) and backend (training RDMA) networks. Its AI-zone backend is a two-stage Clos; larger DC-scale networks add an aggregator tier and are oversubscribed across zones. The paper covers Grand Teton/H100-era infrastructure, production workloads, and clusters scaling to thousands of GPUs; it is not a claim that every Meta cluster uses one universal rail arrangement. **[observed]** [Meta, *RDMA over Ethernet for Distributed AI Training at Meta Scale*, §§2–3](https://cs.stanford.edu/~keithw/sigcomm2024/sigcomm24-final246-acmpaginated.pdf)

Meta’s operational account is especially useful diagnostically: default ECMP performed poorly with low-entropy, bursty collective flows; path pinning could be imbalanced under partial rack allocation or failures; traffic engineering improved controlled 128-node benchmarks by 5–10% over E-ECMP, but added complexity and could be less resilient under multiple link failures. E-ECMP was chosen at DC scale as a tradeoff. These are deployment-specific measured results, not a universal routing prescription. **[observed]** [Meta paper, §§4.1–4.4](https://cs.stanford.edu/~keithw/sigcomm2024/sigcomm24-final246-acmpaginated.pdf)

Meta’s observable symptoms include NIC out-of-sequence (OOS) packets, link-flap counts and local-ACK-timeout (LAT) counts; their paper says OOS identified packet drops that were not visible in other metrics. It also describes monitoring long PFC pauses, buffer utilization and congestion drops. A turn-up performance regression was ultimately switch-image scheduling latency, despite no monitored congestion metric crossing baseline. This argues for measuring latency and collective outcomes, not counters alone. **[observed]** [Meta paper, §§6.3–6.4](https://cs.stanford.edu/~keithw/sigcomm2024/sigcomm24-final246-acmpaginated.pdf)

### 2.2 DeepSeek: identify the multi-plane topology as V3/R1-era, not an older report

The primary source is the 2025 ISCA paper *Insights into DeepSeek-V3: Scaling Challenges and Reflections on Hardware for AI Architectures*. It explicitly describes DeepSeek-V3 trained on 2,048 H800 GPUs and its infrastructure as an eight-plane, two-layer Multi-Plane Fat-Tree (MPFT): eight GPU/NIC pairs per node, each assigned to a distinct IB plane, plus a separate 400-Gb/s RoCE storage-network plane. The paper says policy/regulatory constraints meant the theoretical 16,384-GPU capacity was not deployed; actual scale was just over 2,000 GPUs. **[observed]** [DeepSeek ISCA’25 paper, §§1, 5.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.09343v1)

That MPFT attribution belongs to V3’s documented H800-era training infrastructure (and the paper discusses V3/R1 architecture); do not back-project it onto DeepSeek’s earlier V2/LLM runs or their different reported hardware. V2 is the 236B MoE model (21B active); V3 is 671B (37B active) and is the report explicitly paired with MPFT. **[observed]** [DeepSeek ISCA’25 paper, §§1–2](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.09343v1)

The topology’s diagnostic implications are concrete: test physical paths independently where exposed, then test aggregate multi-plane behavior and cross-plane forwarding. Do not equate plane with rail: multiple physical planes may be fused beneath one logical HCA/rail; enumerate device, port, plane, and rail mappings. DeepSeek reports near-equivalent MPFT/MRFT all-to-all results from 32–128 GPUs, >40 GB/s per GPU in its DeepEP EP pattern, and similar V3 training metrics at 2,048 GPUs within normal variation. But current CX7 implementation did not realize the ideal single logical NIC across planes; cross-plane traffic required forwarding inside the node and could add latency. The paper does not report a deliberately broken-plane experiment; that diagnostic implication is an inference, not an observed failure result. **[inference]** [DeepSeek paper, §§5.1–5.1.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.09343v1)

DeepSeek also reports a distinct V3 design response to scale-up/scale-out disparity: node-limited expert routing reduces the number of nodes a token targets, thereby reducing IB traffic. Avoid using that optimized model pattern as the sole fabric test: it can suppress network demand that a general all-to-all or all-rank collective exposes. **[observed + inference]** [DeepSeek paper, §4.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.09343v1)

## 3. Collective bring-up: diagnose connectivity, topology, and performance separately

NCCL’s own environment documentation makes rail intent explicit and separately describes rail/plane identifiers; a physical plane need not correspond one-to-one with a logical rail/HCA. Record physical cabling-to-device mapping rather than infer it from NCCL terminology. `NCCL_CROSS_NIC=0` keeps corresponding ring/tree traffic on the same NIC and suits per-NIC switch rails; `1` allows cross-NIC and suits fabrics where all NICs land on a common switch; default `2` tries same-NIC but can cross when beneficial. `NCCL_IB_HCA` can explicitly select HCAs and assign rail/plane identities. Thus a bring-up test should record detected topology and effective NCCL selection, not infer correct rail mapping from a successful job. **[observed]** [NVIDIA NCCL environment variables: CROSS_NIC, IB_HCA](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/env.html)

A practical certification matrix, **[inference]** from production patterns and the rack-bench contract:

1. **Bootstrap/connectivity:** launch a small two-rank GPU collective per representative pair; record initialization, selected transport/HCA, timeouts and completion. Intra-rack NVL72 ranks may communicate over NVLink (or multi-node NVLink/MNNVL), so successful intra-rack NCCL alone does not prove scale-out RDMA. For an RDMA-only result, record the NCCL NVLink/MNNVL policy and prove the actual transport/HCA plus relevant NIC counter deltas; otherwise use a cross-rack peer. A PASS must establish the intended path, not merely socket fallback. Covers wrong GID/route, dead path, bad rankfile, plugin/fallback and hangs. [NCCL env docs](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/env.html)
2. **Per-link/per-rail:** run RDMA read/write perftest and a GPU-buffer test on each mapped rail/port; compare measured throughput and latency with the same-rack peer distribution and link rate. Test one rail at a time, then all rails, to reveal dead links and asymmetry hidden by striping. [Meta paper](https://cs.stanford.edu/~keithw/sigcomm2024/sigcomm24-final246-acmpaginated.pdf)
3. **Collective-pattern × size sweep:** at small, medium, and large message sizes, execute all-reduce (DDP), reduce-scatter + all-gather (FSDP), and all-to-all (MoE/EP), including latency-size and bandwidth-size behavior; use both MPI-launch and framework path where feasible. Meta documents these as distinct traffic patterns: all-to-all full-mesh/incast; all-reduce tree/ring; FSDP ring gather/scatter. [Meta paper, §2.2](https://cs.stanford.edu/~keithw/sigcomm2024/sigcomm24-final246-acmpaginated.pdf) [NVIDIA NCCL collectives](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/usage/collectives.html)
4. **Rank placement and scale:** compare same-tray, cross-tray, rail-aligned and topology-spanning rank assignments; progress from a small subset to the whole 18-tray NVL72 acceptance unit. Track per-rank completion and tail, not only global average. Meta reports topology-aware rank assignment and scheduler placement as performance-relevant. [Meta paper, §§3.3, 6.1](https://cs.stanford.edu/~keithw/sigcomm2024/sigcomm24-final246-acmpaginated.pdf)
5. **Before/after evidence:** snapshot NIC counters, link state/speed, switch counters when available, NCCL logs and GPU/CPU telemetry; diff counters around each test. OOS/LAT/link flap are especially actionable Meta signals. Preserve versions/configuration with results. [Meta paper, §6.3](https://cs.stanford.edu/~keithw/sigcomm2024/sigcomm24-final246-acmpaginated.pdf)

A matrix is valuable because a single all-reduce score is underdetermined: the chosen collective algorithm, message size, rank placement and rail use alter traffic and bottleneck. NCCL itself chooses algorithm/protocol based on topology and size, and documents debugging overrides as temporary diagnostic tools, not production settings. Avoid “fixing” certification by forcing an algorithm/protocol unless the run is explicitly a controlled comparison. **[inference]** [NVIDIA NCCL env docs](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/env.html) [Meta paper, §2.2](https://cs.stanford.edu/~keithw/sigcomm2024/sigcomm24-final246-acmpaginated.pdf)

## 4. Straggler attribution: communication wait is a clue, not a verdict

Synchronous training waits at synchronization points. PyTorch’s DDP straggler guidance shows that one rank can report an unusually long all-reduce because it arrived early and waited for slower ranks; another rank may have short synchronization time precisely because it was the straggler and entered late. Their documented causes include outlier data examples, variable data I/O/transforms, and imbalanced pre-sync computation. Therefore gradient-sync duration alone cannot identify a network fault. **[observed]** [PyTorch, *Straggler Mitigation on PyTorch DDP*](https://pytorch.org/blog/straggler-mitigation)

Attribute using synchronized rank timelines: compare forward/backward or “ready-to-communicate” timestamps, collective entry/exit, exposed wait, GPU clocks/utilization/throttle/ECC, CPU/proxy thread scheduling and utilization, and data-loader batch-ready times. A fabric suspect is stronger when a rank is ready on time but its collective progress/completion is late, repeats by HCA/rail or path, and coincides with network error/counter deltas. A late collective entry after slow compute/data loading, or host proxy starvation with clean link signals, points away from the fabric. These are diagnostic rules synthesized from the causal distinctions in the sources, not a guaranteed root-cause classifier. **[inference]** [PyTorch](https://pytorch.org/blog/straggler-mitigation) [Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/compute/stragglers-in-ai-a-guide-to-automated-straggler-detection) [Meta paper, §6.3](https://cs.stanford.edu/~keithw/sigcomm2024/sigcomm24-final246-acmpaginated.pdf)

Google’s production straggler service describes passive traffic observation to construct a directed communication graph, then causal traversal to distinguish a node that is waiting from the original source of delay. Its post reports deployment on 8,000-GPU Magic workload and reduction of localization from days to minutes, but is vendor-authored and does not disclose the full algorithm or controlled evaluation. It illustrates the scale-practice direction: correlate dependencies across ranks, rather than rank nodes by isolated utilization or RTT. **[observed; vendor-reported impact]** [Google Cloud straggler detection](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/compute/stragglers-in-ai-a-guide-to-automated-straggler-detection)

### 4.1 Communication/compute overlap limits interpretation

DeepSeek V3/R1 uses DualPipe to overlap attention/MoE computation with MoE communication and reports dual-microbatch overlap in inference; the paper also notes communication work can consume GPU SMs (up to 20 SMs in its described training case) for message handling, forwarding, copies, reductions and casts. It says inference can use NIC RDMA all-to-all to avoid some SM contention. Thus observed step time is not simply network time: hidden communication may be masked by compute until communication exceeds the overlap window; conversely, network/proxy work can steal GPU/CPU resources and reduce compute. **[observed]** [DeepSeek paper, §§2.3.1, 4.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.09343v1)

For a short certification, use explicit standalone collectives to isolate fabric capacity, followed by a short representative compute+collective overlap probe to detect gross interference. Compare exposed communication time and end-to-end step time; do not label a hidden/overlapped communication phase “zero network cost.” Full workload traces, rare stragglers and long-tail causal attribution need longer real jobs/telemetry. **[inference]** [DeepSeek paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.09343v1) [PyTorch DDP](https://pytorch.org/blog/straggler-mitigation)

## 5. Candidate two-hour bench versus longer smoke

A plausible two-hour allocation for one certification unit (18 trays) is **[inference]**, contingent on compiled test tools, controlled scheduling and parallel execution:

- 0–10 min: topology/rank/HCA/rail manifest and counter baselines; verify all 18 trays participate.
- 10–25 min: NCCL initialization/connectivity canary and per-rail RDMA probes in parallel, with a small sampled pair set plus every tray’s mapped links.
- 25–75 min: collective matrix (all-reduce, all-gather/reduce-scatter, all-to-all; latency and bandwidth sizes), first on rail-aware placements, then rack-spanning ranks; retain per-rank distributions and repeat outliers.
- 75–100 min: full-rack aggregate saturation and deliberate concurrent collectives to surface contention/imbalance; sample counters during load.
- 100–115 min: brief compute+communication overlap run with data resident in memory and fixed workload; collect GPU/CPU/loader timings for attribution.
- 115–120 min: counter deltas, artifact completeness, deterministic rerun of failures.

Bench should fail on non-completing collectives, missing expected ranks/rails, measured per-link/collective results below profile thresholds, severe rank/rail asymmetry, error-counter increments attributable to fabric, or a result that silently used an unintended fallback. Thresholds should be model/rank-count/topology calibrated; no public primary source supplies universal GB300 acceptance numbers. **[inference]** [NVIDIA NCCL docs](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/env.html) [rack-bench README, `bench network`, lines 327–337](../../README.md#L327-L337)

Longer smoke is needed for intermittent link retrains, rare packet drops/timeouts, cumulative counter growth, thermal/power effects, PFC deadlock/watchdog events, and failures that emerge only under sustained concurrent GPU+network load. Meta describes rare drops, link flaps, LAT and interactions among firmware, bursty jobs and buffer bugs; rack-bench README assigns sustained RDMA/TCP mesh and GPU+interconnect concurrent stress to smoke. Two hours can screen and localize obvious defects, not prove reliability over days or certify every production model’s traffic mix. **[observed + inference]** [Meta paper, §§5–6](https://cs.stanford.edu/~keithw/sigcomm2024/sigcomm24-final246-acmpaginated.pdf) [rack-bench README, Stage 3 smoke, lines 478–493](../../README.md#L478-L493)

## 6. Evidence limits and interpretation

The rack-bench README is a design specification, not evidence that network bench is implemented or that listed tests have been run. It proposes 8B–16GB collectives, matrix samples, line-rate comparison and a multi-node rankfile path; this research adds AI-lab diagnostic rationale, not empirical GB300 thresholds. **[observed]** [rack-bench README, lines 327–337](../../README.md#L327-L337)

Meta’s publication is unusually rich primary operational evidence but describes its RoCE clusters and platforms, not an NVL72 GB300 rack. DeepSeek’s MPFT evidence concerns H800/V3 and cannot establish GB300 performance. README lines 335–337 specify N-node collectives for scale-out; an intra-rack NVL72-only collective may remain on NVLink/MNNVL and is not RDMA-path evidence without transport/HCA/counter proof or a cross-rack peer. PyTorch’s example demonstrates attribution pitfalls, not a universal detection algorithm. Google’s causal system is a vendor description with limited public implementation detail. These limits should constrain claims and thresholds. **[inference]** [Meta](https://cs.stanford.edu/~keithw/sigcomm2024/sigcomm24-final246-acmpaginated.pdf) [DeepSeek](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.09343v1) [PyTorch](https://pytorch.org/blog/straggler-mitigation) [Google](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/compute/stragglers-in-ai-a-guide-to-automated-straggler-detection)

## Gaps

- No public source here provides validated per-rail, per-collective GB300/NVL72 pass thresholds or a tested two-hour schedule; rack-bench’s profile must derive thresholds from verified platform/vendor specifications and measured healthy-rack baselines.
- DeepSeek’s report establishes V3/H800 MPFT and V3/R1-era context, but does not show that all later DeepSeek deployments use this same fabric; topology claims should remain version- and run-specific.
- Meta’s counters and routing lessons do not establish which equivalents are exposed on a GB300/NVIDIA fabric management stack; switch-side access/telemetry permissions may be absent.
- Public straggler writeups do not expose enough implementation detail to reproduce Google’s causal graph system. A rack bench can capture causal-friendly timestamps and counters, but robust fleet-wide diagnosis needs job telemetry and historical baselines.
- The proposed matrix is a candidate design, not a schedule benchmarked against actual 18-tray GB300 setup/teardown overhead. Concurrent runs may contend with one another and invalidate isolation; exact orchestration and run ordering require hardware validation.

# Books and canonical references for east-west fabric diagnosis

Research date: 2026-10-11. All claims below carry a source URL.

Scope: N07 only. Which references best support diagnosis of east-west fabric quality during a two-hour GB300 NVL72-class (18-tray) rack certification? Focus is books and primary technical references, not implementation of the suite. The needed evidence includes 8 B–16 GB NCCL/RCCL collectives, per-rail RDMA bandwidth/latency, line-rate normalization, dead or asymmetric rails, topology/routing, congestion (ECN/PFC), errors/retries, and SHARP. North-south internet/storage are out of scope. The sibling canon exemplar is `.../research-internet/.lavish/internet-research/books.md`; project `README.md` is read-only.

## 1. Ranked canon: books, honestly scoped

Few books directly diagnose modern GPU RDMA fabrics. The highest-value “canon” is a short systems-performance book plus current vendor/tool documentation. Books supply reasoning; they do not replace firmware-specific counter definitions, switch telemetry, or contemporary NCCL guidance. [inference] [NCCL networking troubleshooting, version 2.31.2](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)

| Rank | Reference | Verdict | What it supports / does not |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Brendan Gregg, *Systems Performance: Enterprise and the Cloud*, 2e (2020), especially chs. 2, 10, 12 | Must-read book | USE (utilization, saturation, errors), network stack and interfaces, experiment discipline, saturation/outlier interpretation. Not a RoCE/IB or NCCL manual. [observed] [Book/TOC](https://www.brendangregg.com/systems-performance-2nd-edition-book.html) |
| 2 | Kurose & Ross, *Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach*, 8e (2021), ch. 1 and transport/network foundations | Skim / fundamentals | Delay, loss, throughput, routing and queueing vocabulary; useful for reasoning about bottlenecks, not GPU RDMA diagnosis or current switch behavior. Its TCP framing must not be mistaken for RDMA transport expertise. [observed] [Pearson](https://www.pearson.com/en-us/subject-catalog/p/computer-networking/P200000003334/9780135928615) |
| 3 | Raj Jain, *The Art of Computer Systems Performance Analysis* (1991), measurement/statistics chapters | Reference, not fabric guide | Experimental design, variance, comparison and reporting discipline for deciding whether rail asymmetry or collective regression is real. Old examples; statistics remain useful. [observed] [Author book page](https://www.cse.wustl.edu/~jain/books/perfbook.htm) |

**Do not rank TCP/IP Illustrated as a core fabric book.** The supplied ISBN 020163354X identifies *Volume 2: The Implementation*, by Gary R. Wright and W. Richard Stevens. Its publisher TOC and preface describe 4.4BSD-Lite code. [observed] [Publisher TOC and preface](https://www.informit.com/store/tcp-ip-illustrated-volume-2-implementation-9780201633542) [Source note](oreilly/tcpip-illustrated.md)

 Its TCP retransmission, congestion and packet-capture concepts help with management-plane/TCP bootstrap failures, but NCCL payload uses verbs/RDMA paths; TCP congestion-control explanations do not diagnose IB/RoCE data-plane quality. Likewise, Kurose & Ross is introductory conceptual background, not a substitute for fabric docs. [inference] [NCCL networking troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)

## 2. Higher-ranked than books: current primary operational canon

1. **NCCL Networking Troubleshooting (NCCL 2.31.2 documentation)** — best concise diagnostic sequence. Check `ibstat`/`ibstatus` for active state, physical link, correct link layer and expected rate; then `ib_write_bw`, `ib_write_lat`, RDMA stats and port counters; use `ibdiagnet` for fabric-wide topology/routing when available. For RoCE, inspect NIC and switch PFC/ECN/CNP/drop telemetry. It explicitly notes `NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX` behavior changed in NCCL 2.21: dynamic GID selection is used in 2.21+, so do not blindly apply older instructions. [observed] [NVIDIA NCCL networking guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)
2. **NCCL diagnostics, tuning, logging, and environment-variable docs** — use actual NCCL logs and version-matched configuration, rather than assume the intended HCA/rail or transport was selected. Force/debug variables can change transport and must not silently contaminate the certified default result. The docs warn `NCCL_IB_DISABLE=1` disables verbs and can make NCCL fall back to sockets; such a run is not an RDMA pass. [observed] [NCCL troubleshooting index](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting.html), [environment variables](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/env.html)
3. **Vendor fabric manuals (NVIDIA/Mellanox plus the actual switch vendor and firmware release)** — authoritative for counter semantics, QoS/priority mapping, PFC watchdogs, ECN thresholds, adaptive routing and SHARP configuration. There is no portable universal command or counter set: firmware, ASIC, OS and management plane determine visibility. NVIDIA ibdiagnet manual documents topology/fabric checks and SHARP counter options; its versioned manual must match deployed tool. [observed] [ibdiagnet 2.11 manual PDF](https://docs.nvidia.com/ibdiagnet-infiniband-fabric-diagnostic-tool-user-manual-v2-11.pdf)
4. **Open tool docs/source: `perftest`, `infiniband-diags`, `rdma-core`** — essential for flags and limitations, but pin exact installed version. `perfquery` retrieves PMA basic/extended counters and optional detail groups; its option availability and counter exposure depend on PMA/device support. [observed] [perfquery(8)](https://manpages.ubuntu.com/manpages/jammy/man8/perfquery.8.html)

## 3. Tools: practical checks and interpretation traps

### Per-rail bandwidth and latency

NCCL documentation recommends the server/client pattern `ib_write_bw -d <device> -a` and matching client invocation; for a rack certification, bind each test to each HCA/port/rail explicitly and record both endpoints, direction, QP count, message geometry, tool version, CPU/NUMA placement and GPU-vs-host memory mode. Add `ib_read_bw`; WRITE alone is not a complete check. Run paired reverse-direction checks to expose asymmetric paths. A microbenchmark verifies that configured endpoint pair and RDMA verb can transfer; it is not equivalent to collective performance or concurrent rack-scale saturation. [observed] [NCCL low-level tests](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html), [perftest README](https://github.com/linux-rdma/perftest)

Current upstream `perftest` documents `-D/--duration=<sec>`, `-f/--margin=<sec>`, `-b/--bidirectional`, `-O/--dualport`, `-q/--qp`, `-d/--ib-dev`, `-i/--ib-port`, `-x/--gid-index`, and `--use_cuda=<gpu_index>` (for supported builds). The server and client must receive the same options; peers should use the same perftest version. CUDA/DMA-BUF options are build-, CUDA-, kernel-, driver- and adapter-dependent; inspect the local `ib_write_bw --help`, and do not infer GB300 support from an older distro man page. [observed] [perftest README](https://github.com/linux-rdma/perftest)

The README says bandwidth tests can use fixed duration, and latency is reported min/median/max; it cautions that latency is RTT divided by two and can misrepresent asymmetric paths. `-a` sweeps sizes 2 through 2^23 in that README, but version-specific implementations can differ. In a two-hour window, use short fixed-duration, explicitly selected sizes/QPs for each rail, not a broad blind sweep as the only evidence. [observed] [perftest methodology](https://github.com/linux-rdma/perftest) [inference]

### Counters, units, deltas, rollover

- InfiniBand `perfquery` queries PMA counters; `PortXmitData` and `PortRcvData` are counts of data octets divided by four: four octets per counter unit. The exact specification text says “Total number of data octets, divided by 4” (Vol. 1, §16.1.3.5, Table 228, printed p. 966, `PortXmitData`; `PortRcvData` follows). Its field width is separately listed as 32 bits. The same section says counters “instead of overflowing, ... shall stop at all ones” (p. 963). Optional Table 241, `PortCountersExtended`, printed pp. 983–984, gives `PortXmitData`/`PortRcvData` 64-bit fields and says their semantics are identical to the base fields. Thus four octets is the data unit, not the counter width; base saturation and extended width are distinct. Convert deltas as `count × 4` octets and verify which attribute the local tool/device exposes. [observed] [IBTA InfiniBand Architecture Specification v1.2.1, §16.1.3.5, Table 228 p. 966 and §16.1.4.11, Table 241 pp. 983–984; quoted text verified from full PDF](https://www.afs.enea.it/asantoro/V1r1_2_1.Release_12062007.pdf) [perfquery(8), extended attribute optional](https://manpages.ubuntu.com/manpages/jammy/man8/perfquery.8.html)
- Sample before/after counters and compute deltas, preferably at several short intervals. A nonzero historical error count does not prove a current fault; growth during a controlled load is evidence. Counter reset is disruptive/destructive to shared observability and should not be used unless approved; do not clear fabric-wide state during certification. [inference] [NCCL counter guidance](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)
- Counter saturation/rollover is real. Red Hat documents older mlx4/mlx5 systems where `port_xmit_data`, `port_rcv_data`, and packet counters stopped at roughly 4.3 billion; the symptom and remedy are stack/version-specific. Prefer extended counters where supported, sample frequently enough to bound wrap, and detect implausible negative/reset deltas. Do not present this historical issue as universal behavior on GB300. [observed] [Red Hat KB](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/1438663)
- RoCE exposes multiple layers: Ethernet NIC counters (`ethtool -S`), RDMA counters (`rdma statistic`/sysfs), and switch per-priority queue/PFC/ECN counters. NVIDIA says inspect port errors/drops/pause/PFC and congestion indicators; growing `rnr_nak_retry_err`, `packet_seq_err`, `implied_nak_seq_err`, or `local_ack_timeout_err` can indicate transport trouble, but counter names/meaning vary across kernel/driver. Collect exact names plus driver/firmware version. [observed] [NCCL guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)
- Oracle’s 2022 counter explainer describes `np_ecn_marked_roce_packets`, `np_cnp_sent`, `rp_cnp_handled`, and `rp_cnp_ignored`: ECN-marking and CNP/reaction activity are valuable congestion evidence. These counters are implementation- and kernel/OFED-dependent; increasing counts alone are not a failure (they can show functioning congestion response). Correlate their deltas with PFC pause time, queue drops, latency tails and throughput. [observed] [Oracle Linux](https://blogs.oracle.com/linux/rocev2-congestion-counters-explained)

### Capture, privilege and topology limits

`ibdump` is an optional troubleshooting capture, not a required pass/fail instrument. Its upstream README warns it can drop bursts beyond 4096 packets without reporting packet loss, may mishandle outbound retransmitted/multicast packets, and may stop capturing when used on the same port as the Subnet Manager. It has adapter/firmware-build compatibility limits; notably ConnectX-4+ support is absent when built without FW tools. The README says the standalone repository will be removed by end-2026 and directs users to obtain `ibdump` from the `mstflint` project. Therefore a clean capture cannot prove a lossless fabric. Use counters and workload results as primary evidence; verify the replacement binary/build locally. [observed] [Mellanox ibdump README and migration notice](https://github.com/Mellanox/ibdump) [mstflint](https://github.com/Mellanox/mstflint)

Host-side unprivileged RDMA verbs may work when device nodes and ulimits permit, but inventory and counter access vary by permissions; `perfquery`, `ibdiagnet`, switch telemetry and firmware interfaces often require elevated privileges or Subnet Manager/management access. NCCL documentation specifically notes `ibdiagnet` fabric-wide diagnostics usually require SM access, and pinned-memory registration failures may require unlimited memlock (verify `ulimit -l`). If access is absent, report the diagnostic as unavailable/limited—not PASS. [observed] [NCCL guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)

## 4. Applying the canon to the two-hour rack window

A practical evidence sequence is: (1) save stack versions and selected HCA/port mapping; (2) capture read-only link state/rates and baseline error counters per rail; (3) run a short, explicit QP sanity test and `ib_write_bw`/`ib_read_bw` in each direction, comparing per-rail rates to physical line rate after protocol overhead; (4) run the prescribed NCCL all-reduce/all-gather/all-to-all sweep over 8 B–16 GB, retaining algorithm bandwidth and bus bandwidth plus actual NCCL transport/plugin logs; (5) sample counters during and after the collective, including per-rail errors/retries, ECN/CNP/PFC and switch queue drops where available; (6) flag dead/slow rails, asymmetric directions, unexpected transport fallback and a jagged message-size curve for investigation. [inference] [NCCL guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html) [local project README](../../README.md#L327-L337)

For line-rate normalization, state whether the denominator is per port, per rail, per direction, or aggregate full-duplex capacity. A 4×200 Gb/s setup is not one 800 Gb/s unidirectional stream unless topology, rail striping and workload actually use all four links. Do not label vendor theoretical rates or configured rail count as measured performance. NCCL's algbw and busbw are distinct quantities; preserve both and use the project's explicitly defined normalization rather than compare unlike figures. [inference] [NCCL tests performance guide](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests)

Two hours is sufficient for targeted diagnostics, not a full combinatorial matrix of every 18-tray pair, all payloads, QP counts, verbs, directions and congestion states. Use all-rail coverage for link health and per-rail microbenchmarks, representative intra-rack pairs, then full-rack NCCL collective sweeps. A sample cannot certify every pair; state coverage and skipped pairs. Keep a later smoke/burn-in phase for intermittent/thermal faults. [inference] [local project README, bench network](../../README.md#L327-L337) [local project README, smoke network and gpu-network](../../README.md#L486-L493)

## 5. Current vendor docs and papers beat books

- **NCCL behavior, GID selection, HCA selection, plugins, logging and algorithm tuning:** version-matched NCCL docs and source are superior to any book. NCCL 2.21 changed dynamic RoCE GID selection; older recipes can be actively misleading. [observed] [NCCL guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)
- **SHARP:** consult the installed HPC-X/NVIDIA SHARP documentation and versioned `ibdiagnet` manual for enablement, aggregation topology and counters. A successful NCCL result alone does not prove SHARP was selected; logs/plugin evidence must show the actual path. SHARP offload is an optional optimization and its capacity/resource allocation is not inferable from generic textbook collective theory. [inference] [ibdiagnet manual](https://docs.nvidia.com/ibdiagnet-infiniband-fabric-diagnostic-tool-user-manual-v2-11.pdf) [NCCL environment variables](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/env.html)
- **RoCE ECN/PFC/DCQCN:** switch-vendor deployment guides and current NVIDIA NIC/firmware docs outrank textbooks because priority mapping, thresholds, counters and congestion algorithms are configuration- and ASIC-specific. PFC can prevent loss but pause propagation/head-of-line effects can suppress throughput; ECN/CNP evidence must be correlated with performance, not scored as “any PFC means fail.” [inference] [Oracle counter explainer](https://blogs.oracle.com/linux/rocev2-congestion-counters-explained) [Arista deployment guide](https://www.arista.com/assets/data/pdf/Arista-Broadcom-AI-Networking-Deployment-Guide.pdf)
- **Adaptive routing and routing validation:** use the exact switch/firmware management manual and fabric manager telemetry; a host endpoint test cannot establish which path was selected or that adaptive routing is active. `ibdiagnet` helps establish topology/route consistency, subject to management-plane access. [inference] [NVIDIA UFM adaptive routing](https://networking-docs.nvidia.com/ufmsdnappswum/41815/adaptive-routing) [ibdiagnet manual](https://docs.nvidia.com/ibdiagnet-infiniband-fabric-diagnostic-tool-user-manual-v2-11.pdf)

## 6. Recommended reading order

1. Read Gregg *Systems Performance* 2e ch. 2, ch. 10, and ch. 12 for method, saturation and benchmark hygiene. [observed] [Gregg book page](https://www.brendangregg.com/systems-performance-2nd-edition-book.html)
2. Read the current NCCL networking troubleshooting and logging/tuning pages end-to-end; map each recommendation to the installed NCCL and plugin version. [observed] [NCCL troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)
3. Read local `ib_write_bw --help`, `ib_read_bw --help`, `perfquery --help` and perftest README for the exact installed binaries. Run non-destructive link checks first; keep client/server command lines matched. [observed] [perftest](https://github.com/linux-rdma/perftest) [perfquery](https://manpages.ubuntu.com/manpages/jammy/man8/perfquery.8.html)
4. Read the exact switch/NIC vendor manuals for topology, counters, PFC/ECN, adaptive routing and SHARP, then verify read access before certification day. [inference] [local project README, audit network telemetry](../../README.md#L220-L239)
5. Use Kurose & Ross ch. 1 for conceptual queueing/throughput gaps, and Jain when designing thresholds/repeat policy. Do not spend certification prep time treating TCP texts as RDMA handbooks. [inference] [Kurose & Ross](https://www.pearson.com/en-us/subject-catalog/p/computer-networking/P200000003334/9780135928615) [Jain](https://www.cse.wustl.edu/~jain/books/perfbook.htm)

## 7. O'Reilly supplement: optional references

[observed] The [eleven-source supplement](oreilly.md) checks edition identity, chapter evidence, access, and portable methods.
Its [source map](oreilly/research.md) retains explicit gaps.
Catalog matches do not establish subscriber access.

Do not turn an inferred technique into an attributed textbook prescription.
No source establishes measured target-rack PASS.
[Supplement](oreilly.md) [NCCL](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)

## Sources

- Kept: [NCCL networking troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html) — NCCL 2.31.2 practical IB/RoCE checklist, version caveats, privilege/access notes.
- Kept: [NCCL troubleshooting index](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting.html) and [NCCL env docs](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/env.html) — version-sensitive behavior and transport selection.
- Kept: [perftest upstream](https://github.com/linux-rdma/perftest) — flags, benchmark methodology, version and GPU-build caveats.
- Kept: [IBTA InfiniBand Architecture Specification v1.2.1](https://www.afs.enea.it/asantoro/V1r1_2_1.Release_12062007.pdf) — primary source, §16.1.3.5, Table 228 p. 966 (base unit/width) and §16.1.4.11, Table 241 pp. 983–984 (extended width). Full PDF text inspected; quote: “Total number of data octets, divided by 4.” [perfquery(8)](https://manpages.ubuntu.com/manpages/jammy/man8/perfquery.8.html) — query operations and optional extended-counter attribute.
- Kept: [ibdiagnet 2.11 manual](https://docs.nvidia.com/ibdiagnet-infiniband-fabric-diagnostic-tool-user-manual-v2-11.pdf) — fabric-wide and SHARP diagnostics.
- Kept: [Oracle RoCE counters](https://blogs.oracle.com/linux/rocev2-congestion-counters-explained) — concrete CNP/ECN counter semantics, with old-version caveat.
- Kept: [Mellanox ibdump README](https://github.com/Mellanox/ibdump) — capture failure modes and end-2026 migration notice to [mstflint](https://github.com/Mellanox/mstflint).
- Kept: [Gregg Systems Performance](https://www.brendangregg.com/systems-performance-2nd-edition-book.html), [Jain](https://www.cse.wustl.edu/~jain/books/perfbook.htm), [Kurose & Ross](https://www.pearson.com/en-us/subject-catalog/p/computer-networking/P200000003334/9780135928615) — ranked book canon.
- Kept: [NVIDIA NCCL tests](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests) — collective benchmark definitions and measured outputs.
- Dropped: TCP-focused texts as core references — useful fundamentals, but not evidence for RDMA verbs, NIC/switch counters or NCCL rail selection.
- Dropped: forums and generic RoCE tutorials — useful incident anecdotes, not authoritative definitions for certification thresholds.

## Gaps

- IBTA specification wording and page references were verified against the full PDF text: Table 228 p. 966 states data octets divided by four and lists the base field as 32 bits; Table 241 pp. 983–984 lists 64-bit extended data fields. Actual extended-counter exposure and device behavior still depend on PMA/device/driver support; verify the selected attribute locally.
- The precise GB300-specific SHARP/NVLS capabilities and required plugin versions depend on the deployed software/fabric release; obtain the exact NVIDIA/HPC-X release manuals and verify runtime selection in NCCL logs.
- The certification host's privilege model and switch/UFM credentials are not established here. Missing access limits claims: host-only counters cannot fully prove fabric-wide routing, PFC or ECN health.
- `perftest` flags evolve; the upstream README is live. Pin and record binary version, inspect local help, and ensure compatible peers. CUDA/DMA-BUF support depends on build and installed driver/kernel/toolchain.
- Two-hour timing feasibility depends on actual rail count, pair sampling, setup overhead and 16 GB collective duration. A pre-run timed dry run is needed to set final coverage without confusing this reading canon with measured rack performance.
