# ClusterMAX 3.0 — East-West Fabric Coverage Research

Research date: 2026-10-11. All claims below carry a source URL.

## 1. Current release and evidence model

### 1.1 Current release [observed]

ClusterMAX 3.0 (September 2026) is the current release; the live homepage lists “3.0 (current)” followed by earlier releases ([release page](https://www.clustermax.ai), [3.0 article](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)). The article requests 32 GPUs (4×8 HGX or 8×4 NVL72), an 800G RoCE or XDR InfiniBand fabric where available, and five days each for Slurm and Kubernetes testing ([3.0 article](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)).

### 1.2 Methodology is not the public CLI [observed]

SemiAnalysis says Audit takes about 15 minutes and is public; Performance imposes pass/fail thresholds using microbenchmarks and real workloads; the rest of the test suite remains internal ([3.0 article](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)). The current `cmax` README describes the released tool as an audit CLI: its initial release is a small subset, and the core audit explicitly does not run planned performance or reliability tests ([public cmax README](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/clustermax)). It excludes performance, reliability, provider-side and scale-out-network evidence ([public cmax README](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/clustermax)). Thus the NCCL and endurance methods below are publicly described proprietary testing, not functionality buyers can invoke through public `cmax` today.

## 2. What the published east-west suite measures

### 2.1 Collectives and message-size sweep [observed]

ClusterMAX says it runs MPI collectives using NCCL or RCCL across 8-byte to 16-GB message sizes. Named operations include all-to-all, all-reduce, and all-gather; it also runs the same workloads through PyTorch `torch.distributed` ([3.0 article](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)). This verifies more than a NIC's nominal rate: it exercises collective algorithms and software launch paths, including latency-sensitive small messages and bandwidth-dominated large messages.

The article establishes MPI and `torch.distributed` as separate launch paths, but does not name two specific MPI implementations or establish that every NCCL/RCCL configuration gets an identical full sweep. **[inference]** A certification harness should record framework, launcher, rank placement, algorithm/protocol, and fabric mode with each result; unlike-for-unlike curves are not a fair comparison.

### 2.2 Normalization, curve shape, and monotonicity [observed / inference]

ClusterMAX tracks collective bandwidth and latency across message sizes and world sizes, but the article does not define a single normalized “goodput-%” headline metric applicable to every collective ([3.0 article](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)). In its Google example, it reports 16-node, 16-GiB all-to-all at 99.5 GB/s with gIB versus 95.3 GB/s with other providers’ setup; NVLink was disabled to isolate scale-out RoCE ([3.0 article](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)). **[calculated]** 99.5 GB/s is approximately 796 Gb/s of reported collective bus bandwidth, but it is not itself a universal line-rate percentage: the usable denominator depends on per-GPU rails, topology, algorithm, and what fraction of traffic crosses the scale-out boundary.

The article calls for a roughly logistic increase with message size and says performance should increase monotonically; its GCP jagged curve exposed a wrong GID initially and then a missing gIB plugin ([3.0 article](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)). **[inference]** Monotonicity is a diagnostic heuristic, not proof of health: collectives can change algorithm/protocol at size thresholds, and topology changes effective bandwidth. Set tolerance bands, preserve raw points, and investigate abrupt regressions rather than failing every local dip unconditionally.

### 2.3 Per-rail RDMA and scale [observed]

They use `ib_write_bw` and `ib_read_bw` per network rail, including host-memory fallback over PCIe to find path-specific problems ([3.0 article](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)). ClusterMAX doubles world size until it has used the whole allocation; it also disables NVLink on GB200/GB300 NVL72 runs to isolate the scale-out fabric ([3.0 article](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)). Results require careful accounting for world size, algorithm, placement relative to the scale-out boundary, and NVLink state ([3.0 article](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)).

The article reports Prime Intellect tests up to 13 nodes on ConnectX-8 after standardizing NCCL bootstrap. Separately, its Google Cloud example reports 16-node, 16-GiB all-to-all results ([3.0 article](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)). **[inference]** Thirteen nodes is Prime Intellect’s example; GCP demonstrates 16 nodes; ClusterMAX’s overall maximum tested scale remains undisclosed. Neither point establishes a universal target or performance at larger scales.

### 2.4 Endurance and concurrent GPU load [observed]

Reliability testing starts with an eight-hour simultaneous GPU-GEMM and network all-to-all burn-in. Monitoring records temperature, power, clock, FLOPs, connectivity, latency, bandwidth, and kernel-ring-buffer errors ([3.0 article](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)). The methodology then describes a further sustained scale-out/scale-up fabric test looping large-message all-to-all, all-gather, and reduce-scatter, reporting average/minimum/maximum bandwidth and collective errors ([3.0 article](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)). The public description does not specify the duration of this second fabric loop.

The eight hours are an endurance/reliability phase, not a two-hour quick performance pass. **[inference]** Within a two-hour rack certification window, the defensible parity target is a bounded representative collective/rail sweep plus telemetry and short repetition—not an equivalent eight-hour endurance claim. Link retrains, packet errors, retries, and collective errors are useful measured signals, but do not alone identify a switch, cable, NIC, or congestion-control root cause.

## 3. What fault injection and teardown actually show

The documented injection methods are GPU-centric: DCGM error injection, synthetic NVIDIA XID/SXID messages written to the kernel log, and PCIe upstream-bridge reset yielding a genuine XID 79; AMD systems receive a UMC RAS error. The team measures detection, drain duration, and return-to-service time ([3.0 article](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)). Separately, they reboot all cluster nodes and time recovery ([3.0 article](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)). In an Oracle MI355X case, per-rail `ib_write`/`ib_read` testing across all eight NICs reached 391 Gb/s on every rail, then wedged the node during RDMA connection-manager teardown. The ports still reported ACTIVE at 400 Gb/s and the node remained Ready; the issue was found after RCCL failures and `dmesg` inspection ([3.0 article](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)). **[inference]** This is direct evidence that peak bandwidth plus link-state/Ready checks can miss a broken post-test control path. A teardown-completion check and post-test canary (e.g. fresh RDMA operation or collective) are valuable complementary gates.

**Correction to README assumption:** the public methodology does not describe deliberate network link-flap injection, switch-port shutdown, or a node kill while collectives are running. Node reboots and GPU error injection are real, but they are not evidence that link-flap/node-kill job-level fabric failover is tested. No such network-fault injection should be attributed to ClusterMAX without further evidence. (The local README makes the stronger claim at lines 504–506; its own coverage statement is not supported by the published description: [local README, lines 497–516](file:///home/avirus/.herdr/worktrees/rack-bench/research-network/README.md#L497).)

## 4. Public criteria and public tool boundary

The official Networking criteria page identifies the dimension as performance, latency, connectivity, RDMA and high-speed interconnects; its rendered public page did not expose a detailed criterion list in the fetched text ([criteria page](https://www.clustermax.ai/criteria/networking)). The 3.0 article nonetheless documents active NCCL/RCCL, RDMA-perftest, scaling, and endurance methods as above ([3.0 article](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)). Do not confuse criteria/checklist items or an audit inventory with those proprietary measurements.

The public CLI's networking profile checks configuration and inventory; the README explicitly says performance/reliability testing is not included and that standalone audits omit scale-out checks ([public cmax README](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/clustermax)). Public sources do not provide its internal benchmark code, raw provider result corpus, exact pass thresholds, sweep timing, or reproducible command lines. A provider rating therefore is not an independently reproducible performance certificate from the open CLI.

## 5. Coverage gaps material to rack certification

1. **PFC/ECN:** ClusterMAX describes observed fabric throughput, latency, collective errors, and monitoring telemetry, but its public methodology does not describe deliberate PFC-storm testing, pause-frame validation, ECN marking/threshold validation, or congestion-control misconfiguration injection ([3.0 article](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)). Call those “not described publicly,” not proven absent from internal methods.
2. **Asymmetry and drift:** Per-rail RDMA tests can reveal a weak rail, and all-pair directed management-network testing is described only for the frontend network. A systematic east-west per-rank/per-rail asymmetry report, cross-node drift baseline, or repeated time-series drift threshold is not described publicly ([3.0 article](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)).
3. **Failure path coverage:** Link flap, switch failure, routing convergence, and collective recovery/job checkpoint behavior during network failure are not described publicly. GPU/XID injection and whole-node reboot are not substitutes ([3.0 article](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)).
4. **Scale limit:** Prime Intellect’s example reaches 13 nodes; GCP’s example reaches 16. The overall maximum tested world size across providers remains undisclosed ([3.0 article](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)).
5. **Diagnostic granularity:** The public article gives selected output and case narratives, but not raw per-rank/per-rail traces, stable thresholds, or the full private results dataset ([3.0 article](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)).

## 6. Two-hour parity takeaways for GB300 NVL72

A two-hour `bench network` can reasonably borrow the most diagnostic quick checks: link/rail state and error counters; per-rail `ib_write_bw`/`ib_read_bw`; small-message latency; representative NCCL all-reduce/all-gather/all-to-all from 8 B through large payloads with both MPI and PyTorch launch paths; bus bandwidth normalized to the expected fabric and topology; and a curve-shape/regression check. Record NVLink-enabled and scale-out-isolated mode distinctly. **[inference]** This selection prioritizes configuration mistakes, missing rails, poor small-message latency, scale-out bottlenecks, and conspicuous asymmetry while leaving longer endurance and fault recovery to `smoke`.

Never claim ClusterMAX equivalence for a two-hour result: its described 8-hour concurrent GPU/network burn-in and additional sustained fabric loop exceed the bench window. Nor should static inventory be presented as measured throughput. Local `README.md` describes this bench target at [lines 327–337](file:///home/avirus/.herdr/worktrees/rack-bench/research-network/README.md#L327) and smoke at [lines 478–493](file:///home/avirus/.herdr/worktrees/rack-bench/research-network/README.md#L478); those are project design targets, not implemented functionality, as stated at [lines 17–22](file:///home/avirus/.herdr/worktrees/rack-bench/research-network/README.md#L17).

The public audit can check configuration and topology; the proprietary ClusterMAX Performance and Reliability phases supply evidence that the audit CLI does not. Neither is equivalent to this project's acceptance rule that PASS means measured and is never vendor-claimed ([cmax README](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/clustermax), [local README, lines 117–130](file:///home/avirus/.herdr/worktrees/rack-bench/research-network/README.md#L117)).

Adjacent slices are covered by the [internet sibling brief](/home/avirus/.herdr/worktrees/rack-bench/research-internet/.lavish/internet-research/clustermax.md) and [storage sibling brief](/home/avirus/rack-bench/.lavish/storage-research/clustermax.md); this brief does not re-derive those topics.

## Gaps

- Public sources do not disclose the private suite's exact commands, thresholds, full provider run artifacts, elapsed time per test, or full scale-out result matrix.
- PFC storms, ECN misconfiguration, fabric route manipulation, link flap, and node kill during a live collective are **not described publicly**; the text cannot establish whether private or provider-specific extensions ever tested them.
- Prime Intellect’s 13-node example and GCP’s 16-node example are both published; the overall maximum remains undisclosed.
- The criteria page's rendered public text did not reveal a full itemized networking list, so this brief relies on the official article for test-method claims, not an inferred scorecard.

# Network bench research: failure modes and bench design

Research date: 2026-10-11.

Seven category briefs support this document:
[neoclouds](../neoclouds.md), [hyperscalers](../hyperscalers.md),
[ai-labs](../ai-labs.md), [large-companies](../large-companies.md),
[clustermax](../clustermax.md), [academia](../academia.md), and [books](../books.md).
Each brief gives primary sources and separates observations, calculations, and inferences.
The tables below give design recommendations, not measured results from the Chennai rack.

Target: GB300 NVL72-class rack, 18 trays, Chennai, India.
Window: two hours for network checks, including setup and report creation.
Scope: east-west fabric. North-south internet and storage checks remain outside this report.
GB300 uses NCCL. RCCL evidence supplies comparisons from AMD systems only.
PASS requires measurements from the target rack.
Provider ratings, advertised rates, and configuration flags cannot supply PASS evidence.

## Why network is next

A healthy port does not prove a healthy collective path.
ClusterMAX reports an Oracle MI355X case with 391 Gb/s on all eight rails.
RDMA teardown then fails, although ports remain ACTIVE at 400 Gb/s.
A post-test connection check therefore adds evidence that peak throughput cannot supply (clustermax §3).

A successful collective also does not prove RDMA use.
Google documents an A4X Max/GB300 subblock with 18 instances and 72 GPUs on NVLink.
Its RoCE network connects different subblocks (hyperscalers §14).
NVL72/MNNVL traffic can use NVLink across trays inside the scale-up domain.
NCCL `busbw` can describe NVLink, PCIe, or network limits.
Record actual transport selection and traffic-counter changes (ai-labs §6; neoclouds §4.2; academia §3).
Use a cross-rack peer when the scale-up domain prevents a valid RDMA test.
Without that peer, report the scale-out limit explicitly.

Public provider material supplies useful configuration and test recipes.
It does not supply a matched GB300 baseline for the Chennai rack (neoclouds §5–6).
ClusterMAX describes private performance tests, not public `cmax` performance commands (clustermax §1, §4).
The project must make its own repeatable evidence path.

## Part 1 — Failure-mode catalog

Each entry gives the evidence, two-hour coverage, and catching check.
“Yes” means the check can find a present fault, not exclude every possible fault.
“Partial” means the certificate must state the missing evidence.

| Failure mode | Evidence and mechanism | 2h | Catching check |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Wrong transport or TCP fallback | NCCL can select an unintended path. EFA uses Libfabric, not ordinary `NET/IB` (hyperscalers §2–5). | Yes | Save plugin/provider logs. Check traffic counters during the test. |
| NVLink mistaken for scale-out RDMA | Same-rack NVL72 traffic can remain inside the NVLink domain (ai-labs §6; neoclouds §4.2). | Partial | Use verified network isolation or a cross-rack peer. Keep production-layout results separate. |
| Missing or downshifted rail | Link inventory alone misses degraded data paths (clustermax §2.3, §3; books §4). | Yes | Check expected ports, negotiated rates, QP creation, and isolated-rail throughput. |
| One slow rail hidden by aggregation | Aggregate bandwidth can conceal unequal paths (academia §3; neoclouds §3–4). | Yes | Save each rail's result before the concurrent-rail result. |
| Directional or RDMA read/write asymmetry | Operation roles and GPU-memory paths differ (academia §6; books §3). | Yes | Match parameters, swap endpoints, and compare host-memory with GPU-memory tests. |
| Wrong GID, HCA, topology file, or plugin | ClusterMAX reports GID/plugin faults; Crusoe supplies topology-specific configuration (clustermax §2.2; neoclouds §2.4). | Yes | Save versions and configuration. Run a fresh QP canary before each test group. |
| Shared uplink, PCIe, or GPU feed limit | Healthy isolated rails need not scale concurrently (academia §3, §6). | Yes | Compare concurrent throughput with the sum of isolated results. Check GPU/NIC locality and host load. |
| Low ECMP entropy or bad placement | Meta reports flow collisions and placement penalties (large-companies §2, §4). | Partial | Repeat different endpoint/rank placements and QP settings. Request route and switch evidence. |
| Queue buildup, incast, or PFC propagation | RoCE congestion mechanisms depend on workload and policy (large-companies §2, §5; academia §2, §5). | Partial | Compare idle and loaded latency. Collect ECN/CNP, pause, drop, and retry counter changes. |
| ECN/PFC configuration error | Host counters can show symptoms but cannot prove switch thresholds (large-companies §5; clustermax §5). | Partial | Request switch configuration and time-correlated telemetry. Do not name the cause without evidence. |
| Rank straggler outside the network | Compute, CPU progress, data loading, and GPU throttling can delay collectives (ai-labs §3–4; academia §6). | Partial | Save rank timing, GPU clocks, CPU load, and transport/counter evidence. |
| Collective-specific congestion | AlltoAll uses a different traffic pattern from AllReduce (academia §3; ai-labs §2). | Yes | Run AllReduce, AllGather, and AlltoAll separately. Keep operation-specific results. |
| Algorithm/protocol transition mistaken for a fault | NCCL can change execution paths across message sizes (academia §3; clustermax §2.2). | Yes | Save algorithm/protocol metadata. Repeat the transition points before assigning failure. |
| Short peak mistaken for stable capacity | Few samples hide intermittent faults and variability (academia §7; clustermax §2.4). | Partial | Use warm-up, timed repeats, sample counts, and a short sustained phase. |
| RDMA teardown or reconnect failure | Oracle's peak-rate result precedes a teardown failure (clustermax §3). | Yes | Require process exit, cleanup completion, and a fresh post-test RDMA/collective canary. |
| Link flap, rerouting, or recovery failure | Meta and NetPilot describe traffic changes after failures (large-companies §2; academia §5). | Partial | Read event history and counter changes. Put approved fault injection in a separate test. |
| SHARP feature mistaken for raw fabric health | SHARP offloads reduction work; support does not prove actual use (neoclouds §3.2; large-companies §4). | Partial | Keep baseline and SHARP results separate. Verify selection before comparing identical runs. |
| Rail/plane naming mistaken for path independence | Logical HCA rails and physical planes describe different topology levels (ai-labs §1, §6; neoclouds §4.2). | Partial | Obtain the physical topology map. Do not infer independent failure domains from names. |
| Stale counters or wrong units | Counter width, saturation, wrap, reset, and data units change interpretation (books §3; academia §7). | Yes | Save timestamps, raw values, units, widths, and reset state. Verify movement during traffic. |
| Software drift or launch-path failure | MPI and PyTorch exercise different launch paths (clustermax §2.1; hyperscalers §2–4). | Yes | Save exact commands, versions, environment, rankfiles, and both launcher canaries. |

### What two hours cannot certify

Two hours cannot supply ClusterMAX's eight-hour concurrent GPU/network endurance evidence (clustermax §2.4).
The window cannot establish fleet-scale behavior beyond the available endpoints (hyperscalers §6; clustermax §5).
It cannot measure a long-term flap rate or exclude rare congestion events (neoclouds §4.2; academia §7).
It cannot prove switch ECN/PFC correctness without switch access (large-companies §5).
It cannot prove job recovery without an approved failure test (clustermax §3, §5; academia §5).
It cannot validate every training workload or transport stack (neoclouds §2.2; ai-labs §3–4).
A NCCL result does not validate UCX/NIXL.
A GB300 result does not validate an AMD/RCCL deployment.

## Part 2 — The suite: `bench network`, evidence-aligned

### 2.1 Measurement rules

Record the test boundary first: scale-up, scale-out, or mixed.
Record expected trays, GPUs, HCAs, ports, link rates, rails, and physical planes.
Record the actual tested endpoints and rank count.
Do not call an 18-tray sample a complete directed-pair matrix.
An 18-tray matrix has 306 directed tray pairs: `18 × 17` [calculated].
A representative sample cannot prove all 306 paths.

Use decimal GB/s and Gb/s explicitly. Keep GiB payload sizes separate.
For point-to-point tests, report payload throughput and the matching directional capacity.
Do not divide one rail's result by all rails' advertised capacity.
Keep send, receive, and bidirectional totals separate.
Do not add duplex totals to a unidirectional denominator.

For collectives, keep elapsed time, `algbw`, and `busbw`.
NCCL-tests defines `algbw = S/t` for the operation's tested payload.
For AllReduce, its correction factor is `2(n−1)/n`.
Each rank sends `2S(n−1)/n` bytes across both ring phases under the ring model.
Each rank receives the same volume.
For AllGather and AlltoAll, use the documented operation-specific factor `(n−1)/n`.
Check the pinned NCCL-tests version and payload definition before calculation (academia §2–3; books §3).
`busbw` is a model-based normalization, not a NIC byte counter.
Compare network-only results with the topology's realizable capacity and measured counter changes.
Keep mixed NVLink/network results out of a simple NIC line-rate percentage.

Set acceptance thresholds in a versioned certification profile.
Use a matched, measured known-good baseline and the target topology.
State the allowable variation, message-size regime, rank count, and minimum sample count.
Do not use universal 60%, 98%, monotonicity, or SHARP-gain rules (academia §7; neoclouds §5).
Curve dips start investigation; they do not automatically prove misconfiguration.

Report sample count, warm-up, duration, median, and variation for repeated points.
Keep within-run samples separate from between-run variation.
Do not report p95 or p99 from NCCL aggregate timing alone.
Do not infer rare-event reliability from a small sample (academia §7).

Linux documents `port_xmit_data` and `port_rcv_data` in four-octet units.
Its sysfs ABI describes these data counters as 64-bit fields.
Base PMA PortCounters differs from optional extended counters (books §3).
The base specification uses saturation, not assumed modulo rollover.
Check the actual exported counter before calculating a change.
Source: [Linux InfiniBand sysfs ABI](https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/ABI/stable/sysfs-class-infiniband).

### 2.2 Proposed two-hour budget

This budget is an engineering estimate, not a measured GB300 schedule.
Validate it on the target rack before making a two-hour product promise.
Do not run competing phases concurrently unless the phase specifically measures contention.

| Minutes | Phase | Required evidence | Source basis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0–10 | Inventory and initial counters | Topology, versions, expected rails, active rates, timestamps, reset state | books §4–6; hyperscalers §5 |
| 10–15 | Transport and QP canaries | Fresh QP, GPU-memory support, actual plugin/provider, rank placement | hyperscalers §2–5; neoclouds §2 |
| 15–35 | Isolated rails | RDMA write/read, both directions, small-message latency, selected sizes | academia §4, §6; clustermax §2.3 |
| 35–45 | Concurrent rails and sampled pairs | Aggregate result, per-rail changes, placement coverage | academia §3; large-companies §4 |
| 45–80 | NCCL sweeps | AllReduce/AllGather/AlltoAll, geometric 8 B–16 GB range, raw logs | clustermax §2.1; academia §3 |
| 80–90 | Launcher and scaling checks | PyTorch canary; representative size/rank points; MPI comparison | ai-labs §2–4; clustermax §2.1, §2.3 |
| 90–100 | Short loaded-latency phase | Latency inflation, throughput change, counters, GPU/CPU state | large-companies §4–5; academia §5–6 |
| 100–110 | Suspect-point repeat or optional SHARP comparison | Repeated evidence; verified feature use; same placement and payload | academia §7; neoclouds §3.2 |
| 110–115 | Cleanup and post-test canaries | Successful exit, fresh connection/collective, final counters | clustermax §3 |
| 115–120 | Certificate | Coverage, results, evidence links, uncertainty, explicit misses | academia §7 |

The budget does not promise two full sweeps through both launchers.
Prioritize the complete NCCL sweep through the primary production launcher.
Use matched representative points through the second launcher.
Report that coverage limit instead of claiming identical full coverage.
A 16 GB point can require more memory than its nominal payload.
Check operation buffers, rank count, available GPU memory, and timeouts before launch.
If resources prevent a point, report SKIP and its reason.

### 2.3 Check and result matrix

The identifiers below are proposed implementation identifiers.
They do not describe existing rack-bench commands.

| Proposed check | Metric | Acceptance evidence | Limit or SKIP condition |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `network.transport` | Plugin/provider, HCA/port, traffic changes | Logs and counters show the intended path | No path proof: no scale-out PASS |
| `network.rail.inventory` | Expected/active ports and rates | Measured inventory matches the profile | Missing physical topology limits diagnosis |
| `network.rail.rdma` | Write/read GB/s; latency; errors | Every required rail meets its matched profile | Unsupported GPU-memory backend: separate host result |
| `network.rail.aggregate` | Concurrent GB/s versus isolated sum | Measured aggregate meets the topology-aware profile | Shared endpoint resources must be declared |
| `network.pair.sample` | Directional matrix and placement | All declared sample pairs meet the profile | Untested pairs remain untested |
| `network.collective.sweep` | Time, algbw, busbw, correctness | Each required operation/size meets the profile | Missing size or operation requires explicit coverage limit |
| `network.collective.scale` | Throughput/time by rank count | Measured ranks and topology match the certificate | No cross-rack peers: no wider scale-out claim |
| `network.launcher` | MPI/PyTorch completion and timing | Actual launch paths complete at declared sizes | Canary coverage is not a second full sweep |
| `network.loaded_latency` | Idle/load latency and throughput change | Profile-specific limits with counter evidence | No switch access limits causal conclusions |
| `network.counters` | Byte/error/pause/ECN/CNP/retry changes | Valid interval, units, widths, reset checks | Missing telemetry is unknown, not zero |
| `network.sharp` | Selected offload and matched on/off result | Actual selection plus measured comparison | Unsupported or unsafe: SKIP; baseline remains separate |
| `network.post_canary` | Cleanup and fresh operation | New QP and collective complete after load | Failure blocks a healthy-completion claim |

Use PASS only for complete, measured acceptance evidence.
Use FAIL for a measured violation of the declared profile.
Use SKIP for an unavailable or unsupported check.
Use INCONCLUSIVE when measurements cannot establish the required result.
Map these proposed states to the project's supported report schema during implementation.
Do not silently convert SKIP or INCONCLUSIVE to PASS.
A missing optional switch check need not fail measured throughput.
It must still limit the certificate's root-cause and configuration claims.

hyperscalers.md:
# Hyperscaler GPU-fabric verification and diagnosis
Research date: 2026-10-11. All claims below carry a source URL.

## 1. Executive answer: what “verified” means

Hyperscaler guidance does not treat a configured NIC, advertised link rate, or successful job launch as proof of a healthy GPU fabric. The reproducible evidence chain is: establish the intended placement/topology and software versions; run a low-level transport test on each physical rail; run NCCL collectives with the production transport and rank layout; inspect NCCL logs to prove the selected transport/plugin; correlate performance and errors with host and switch counters. This distinction matters: a NCCL benchmark that silently uses sockets can complete while failing to certify RDMA. **[inference]** [AWS EFA/NCCL test guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html); [NVIDIA NCCL troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting.html)

For rack-bench, a two-hour category can credibly certify a 1-rack NVL72’s host-visible fabric and a representative full-rack collective, but cannot prove large-cluster scale, fabric behavior under long-duration congestion, switch-side ECN/PFC correctness when switch telemetry is inaccessible, or fault recovery under sustained jobs. Those should be explicit evidence boundaries, not implied PASSes. **[inference]** [rack-bench README](../../README.md#L327-L337); [NVIDIA NCCL troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting.html)

## 2. Provider stacks are not interchangeable

### 2.1 AWS EFA: Libfabric provider, not verbs InfiniBand

AWS’s documented EFA path is NCCL through the `aws-ofi-nccl` plugin into Libfabric’s EFA provider (`FI_PROVIDER=efa`); it is not the verbs-based `NET/IB` path used by conventional InfiniBand/RoCE diagnostics. AWS instructs `fi_info -p efa -t FI_EP_RDM` to enumerate the provider and shows NCCL log evidence `NET/OFI Selected Provider is efa`. **[observed]** [AWS EFA/NCCL guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html)

The current AWS page (consulted 2026-10-11) specifies EFA installer `1.50.0`, NCCL source tag `v2.30.4-1`, supported base images including AL2023, Ubuntu 22.04/24.04/26.04, Debian 12/13, RHEL 10, and EFA support from NCCL 2.4.2 onward. The installer command shown is `sudo ./efa_installer.sh -y --mpi=openmpi5`; since EFA 1.30.0 Open MPI 4.1 and 5 are installed by default, with Open MPI 5 alone recommended unless 4.1 is needed. **[observed]** [AWS EFA/NCCL guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html)

The documented NCCL launch explicitly exports `FI_EFA_USE_DEVICE_RDMA=1`, `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO`, an EFA-inclusive `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`; excludes MPI’s `cm` PML, selects TCP/self BTL, and excludes `lo,docker0` from TCP BTL. A positive run logs `NET/OFI Selected Provider is efa`; AWS also gives `NCCL_TOPO_FILE` auto-selection evidence for P4d. This verifies plugin/provider selection, but is not by itself proof of direct GPU memory transfers or per-rail balance. **[observed]** [AWS EFA/NCCL guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html)

AWS’s complete published launch command is reproduced below; it makes transport/configuration reproducible, but the `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` paths depend on the image (AWS docs show `/opt/amazon/efa/lib` here):

```bash
/opt/amazon/openmpi/bin/mpirun \
  -x FI_EFA_USE_DEVICE_RDMA=1 \
  -x LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/opt/nccl/build/lib:/usr/local/cuda/lib64:/opt/amazon/efa/lib:/opt/amazon/openmpi/lib:/opt/amazon/ofi-nccl/lib:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH \
  -x NCCL_DEBUG=INFO \
  --hostfile my-hosts -n 8 -N 8 \
  --mca pml ^cm --mca btl tcp,self --mca btl_tcp_if_exclude lo,docker0 --bind-to none \
  $HOME/nccl-tests/build/all_reduce_perf -b 8 -e 1G -f 2 -g 1 -c 1 -n 100
```

**[observed]** [AWS EFA/NCCL guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html)

AWS recommends cluster placement groups for low-latency placement in one AZ, but says they are not an absolute requirement. EFA security-group self-referencing ingress/egress is mandatory in the documented setup. Placement is therefore a controlled variable for meaningful comparison, not an inference that all racks need a cloud placement-group analogue. **[observed/inference]** [AWS EFA/NCCL guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html)

AWS’s current guide shows an allreduce test at 8 bytes to 1 GiB, doubling (`-f 2`), 8 ranks on an 8-GPU instance, 100 iterations. This is an executable bootstrap example, not sufficient for rack-bench’s full 8 B–16 GB matrix, collective diversity, per-rail RDMA, or full 18-tray rank coverage. **[observed/inference]** [AWS EFA/NCCL guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html)

### 2.2 Azure ND H100/H200: verbs InfiniBand and GPUDirect RDMA

Azure ND H200 v5 is eight H200 GPUs per VM, 900 GB/s NVLink, eight 400-Gbps Quantum-2 ConnectX-7 InfiniBand connections (one per GPU), and 3.2 Tb/s aggregate VM interconnect. Azure describes automatic inter-VM IB configuration for VMs within the same VM scale set and GPUDirect RDMA support. This is a verbs/IB fabric, not EFA/Libfabric. **[observed]** [Azure ND H200 v5 specifications](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/sizes/gpu-accelerated/nd-h200-v5-series)

An Azure community troubleshooting article reports a useful symptom: NCCL showing `NET/Socket` instead of `NET/IB` signals a transport fallback; it advises `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO`, checking OFED (`ofed_info`), interface state (`ibstat`), and same placement group. Treat this as field guidance, not a Microsoft product guarantee. Do not adopt the article’s stated 380+ Gb/s target as a universal acceptance threshold: it refers to a particular H100/cloud configuration and message scale, whereas measured useful throughput depends on GPU/rank count, collective, rail use, message size, and protocol overhead. **[observed/inference]** [Microsoft Community troubleshooting article](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/startupsatmicrosoftblog/your-h100s-on-azure-wont-do-distributed-training-heres-probably-why-/4537502)

Do not conflate ND HN (H100) and H200 claims or assume every ND SKU has the same rank topology. The H200 official specification is explicit for eight GPUs and eight 400-Gbps links; validate SKU-specific topology and fabric arrangement from the deployed offer and inventory before interpreting rates. **[inference]** [Azure ND H200 v5 specifications](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/sizes/gpu-accelerated/nd-h200-v5-series)

### 2.3 Google A3: TCPX/TCPXO GPUDirect plugins; variant matters

Google’s current GPUDirect setup distinguishes A3 Mega (`a3-megagpu-8g`, H100) using GPUDirect-TCPXO (RDMA-like/offloaded stack) from A3 High and A3 Edge (`a3-highgpu-8g`, `a3-edgegpu-8g`, H100) using GPUDirect-TCPX (optimized guest TCP). These are neither AWS EFA nor conventional `NET/IB`; the NCCL plugin and its initialization log are the proof point. Google’s documented network maxima are up to 1,800 Gbps, but that is an advertised ceiling, not a certification result. **[observed]** [Google GPUDirect setup](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/gpus/gpudirect)

Topology differs: A3 Mega requires eight data networks/interfaces plus management; High/Edge require four data networks plus management. Google’s setup configures MTU 8244 and recommends large MTU; High/Edge NICs are NUMA aligned to GPU pairs. The documented test runs `all_gather_perf` through a wrapper across two VMs; one example is `/scripts/run-allgather.sh 8 eth1,eth2,eth3,eth4 1M 512M 2`, taking about two minutes, and successful TCPX initialization is identified by `NCCL INFO NET/GPUDirectTCPX ver. 3.1.1.` **[observed]** [Google GPUDirect setup](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/gpus/gpudirect)

The same Google page’s Mega instructions pin sample RxDM image `v1.0.21` and plugin image `v1.0.15`; these are examples on a mutable “latest” documentation page, not a durable compatibility promise. Capture actual image digests, NCCL/plugin versions, driver, kernel and NIC mapping in rack-bench artifacts; never transplant those GCP version pins onto GB300. **[observed/inference]** [Google GPUDirect setup](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/gpus/gpudirect)

A separate GKE guide limits GPUDirect-TCPX/TCPXO to specific machine types and excludes MIG, time-sharing, MPS, NCCL FastSocket, partial GPU use, and multiple pods sharing the node. Those are product-specific constraints, not general NCCL laws; certification must match its target deployment mode. **[observed]** [GKE GPUDirect bandwidth guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/gpu-bandwidth-gpudirect-tcpx)

## 3. Evidence ladder: isolate transport before NCCL tuning

1. **Prove inventory and rail identity.** Record NIC PCI BDF, firmware, driver/OFED or rdma-core, link state/speed, port errors, NUMA/GPU locality, interface-to-rail mapping, and expected topology. A line-rate readout is a denominator, never a measured PASS. **[inference]** [rack-bench README](../../README.md#L170-L241); [NVIDIA networking troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)
2. **Prove transport discovery and GDR prerequisites.** For EFA run `fi_info -p efa -t FI_EP_RDM`; verify NCCL says `NET/OFI` and `efa`. For IB/RoCE inspect RDMA devices and link state and NCCL’s selected `NET/IB` transport; check GPU peer-memory/DMABUF path and topology. NVIDIA identifies `nvidia-peermem`, compatible drivers/devices and GPU/NIC topology as relevant GDR conditions. **[observed]** [AWS EFA guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html); [NVIDIA GPU troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/gpu_troubleshooting.html)
3. **Run point-to-point RDMA separately from collectives.** For verbs IB/RoCE, `ib_write_bw`/`ib_read_bw` and latency tests per HCA/rail localize link/PCIe/rail issues without NCCL algorithm confounders. EFA uses SRD and has extended verbs support; perftest may be usable only when the installed EFA-capable build explicitly supports the EFA/SRD mode. Do not assume a conventional RC verbs recipe is valid for EFA; verify the device and transport mode in that build and use the AWS/EFA documented method. **[observed/inference]** [AWS EFA guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html); [AWS re:Invent EFA transport slides](https://d1.awsstatic.com/onedam/marketing-channels/website/aws/en_US/events/approved/reinvent-2025/reinvent/2024/slides/cmp/CMP335_Drilling-down-into-performance-for-distributed-training.pdf) Pair tests both directions and preserve raw command, HCA, message size, GID/MTU and counter deltas. **[inference]** [NVIDIA networking troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html); [rack-bench README](../../README.md#L327-L337)
4. **Run workload collectives and verify logs.** `nccl-tests` all-reduce/all-gather/reduce-scatter/all-to-all across tiny through large payloads expose latency, collective efficiency, algorithm/protocol thresholds and scale behavior. Prove intended plugin/transport and selected network interfaces in logs. A complete run over sockets is not a PASS for an RDMA fabric. **[inference]** [NVIDIA nccl-tests](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests); [AWS EFA guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html); [Google GPUDirect setup](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/gpus/gpudirect)
5. **Normalize correctly.** Preserve NCCL `algbw` and `busbw` separately. `algbw` is application algorithm throughput; `busbw` normalizes collective data movement and is the better comparison to effective fabric capacity, but still must be compared to a declared, topology-aware denominator (aggregate bandwidth actually available to ranks, not sum of every port if topology cannot use them all). Report percentage and raw GB/s; do not treat vendor advertised aggregate or a single cloud blog’s percentage as a universal gate. **[inference]** [NVIDIA nccl-tests performance notes](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests); [rack-bench README](../../README.md#L327-L337)

## 4. NCCL controls: evidence, versioning, and restraint

`NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` is a high-value diagnostic for selected transport, plugin, interface, rank mapping, and fallback. It belongs in a bounded diagnostic run and archived logs; verbose logging can perturb timings. Pin exact NCCL, CUDA, driver, MPI, plugin and fabric driver versions alongside results. AWS example currently builds NCCL `v2.30.4-1`; the troubleshooting index labels 2.32.3, while its linked networking subpage labels 2.31.2; preserve each source page version rather than treating them as one release. These are source snapshots, not a recommendation to mix them or a promise they are the newest compatible GB300 stack. **[observed/inference]** [AWS EFA guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html); [NVIDIA troubleshooting index (2.32.3)](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting.html); [networking subpage (2.31.2)](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)

For ordinary verbs IB/RoCE, variables such as `NCCL_IB_HCA` (select devices), `NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX` (RoCE GID selection), `NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME`, and `NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL` can help isolate path selection/GDR. Values and semantics are NCCL-version-sensitive: consult the version-matched environment-variable reference before pinning. Do not globally force HCA/GID/GDR values just because a blog suggests them; first capture the default-selected path, then use one-variable A/B diagnostics. **[inference]** [NCCL environment variables](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/env.html); [NCCL troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting.html)

AWS EFA requires its own control namespace: `FI_EFA_USE_DEVICE_RDMA=1` in AWS’s example, and Libfabric `FI_*` controls are not aliases for `NCCL_IB_*`. GCP TCPX/TCPXO uses Google plugin binaries and wrapper/runtime setup, not verbs tuning. **[observed]** [AWS EFA guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html); [Google GPUDirect setup](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/gpus/gpudirect)

Avoid declaring tuning flags as certification defaults: forced `NCCL_ALGO`, `NCCL_PROTO`, channel counts, PXN, or SHARP can mask auto-selection/topology errors and may be deprecated or have changed semantics in later releases. Capture an untuned baseline first; then diagnostic A/B with exact version and remove overrides for the acceptance result unless the profile intentionally certifies a pinned production configuration. NVIDIA’s troubleshooting structure explicitly puts basic diagnostics before tuning. **[inference]** [NVIDIA NCCL troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting.html); [NCCL environment variables](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/env.html)

No inspected primary hyperscaler source provided a validated GB300-specific `NCCL_IB_QPS_PER_CONNECTION`, ECN/PFC thresholds, adaptive-routing settings, or SHARP acceptance recipe. Treat those as fabric-vendor/controller configuration and telemetry tasks, not guessed NCCL knobs. Current NCCL configuration and legacy/deprecated controls must be checked against the pinned NCCL release; this evidence set does not establish a complete deprecation table. **[inference]** [NVIDIA NCCL environment variables](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/env.html); [NVIDIA networking troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)

## 5. Fault localization matrix

| Observation | First diagnosis | Evidence / interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| NCCL completes but uses `NET/Socket` instead of intended RDMA/plugin | Wrong/missing interface, device, plugin/library path, policy/placement; classify as transport fallback, not fabric PASS | Azure troubleshooting advises `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO`, OFED and `ibstat`; AWS requires explicit `NET/OFI ... efa` provider evidence. **[observed]** [Azure troubleshooting](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/startupsatmicrosoftblog/your-h100s-on-azure-wont-do-distributed-training-heres-probably-why-/4537502); [AWS guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html) |
| Per-rail RDMA rates differ materially | Port/link/optic, PCIe locality, wrong HCA binding, rail mapping, asymmetric route or counter errors; test both directions and inspect per-port deltas | Per-rail pairing is a diagnostic design recommendation, not a cloud-published universal threshold. **[inference]** [NVIDIA networking troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html) |
| RDMA point-to-point healthy; NCCL collective low | Rankfile/GPU-NIC locality, plugin selection, algorithm/protocol, shared rail contention, collective scaling or CPU/progress bottleneck | Separate transport and collective layers; preserve per-message-size curves. **[inference]** [NVIDIA NCCL troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting.html) |
| One message-size band or collective alone degrades | Algorithm/protocol transition, latency floor, rendezvous, rail imbalance, congestion; compare allreduce/allgather/alltoall and logs | Rack-bench README explicitly plans 8 B–16 GB sweeps and monotonicity diagnostics. That monotonicity is a heuristic, not a physical law (algorithm transitions can produce steps). **[observed/inference]** [rack-bench README](../../README.md#L327-L337) |
| Retries/timeouts/errors or throughput collapse under concurrency | Link/fabric errors, congestion, loss, ECN/PFC pause or buffer behavior; take before/after host and switch counters | Host counters alone cannot prove switch queue congestion, ECN marking, PFC storms, or route/adaptive-routing choices. Those require switch/UFM/vendor telemetry. **[inference]** [NVIDIA networking troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html) |
| Hang rather than clean failure | MPI/bootstrap/control-plane reachability, incompatible network selection, blocked ports, bad peer setup, runtime/shared-memory issue; bounded timeout and per-rank logs | AWS EFA self-referencing security-group rules are mandatory; NCCL docs separate runtime/MPI and networking troubleshooting. **[observed]** [AWS guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html); [NVIDIA troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting.html) |

## 6. Fabric features and what a short test can actually establish

**ECN/PFC/congestion:** verify configured intent and counter deltas under a controlled concurrent test. On RoCE, host-side counters can reveal symptoms, but validating switch marking thresholds, pause propagation, headroom, queue drops, and pause storms needs switch telemetry/config. A quiet counter during a brief unloaded run does not establish congestion safety. **[inference]** [NVIDIA networking troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)

**Adaptive routing and SHARP:** test operational availability through the installed fabric manager/plugin and logs, and compare enabled/disabled only as a diagnostic when supported. Hyperscaler sources examined here do not publish enough details to assert a portable SHARP activation command, adaptive-routing proof, or acceptance threshold. Switch/controller evidence must be sourced from the deployed fabric vendor. **[inference]** [NVIDIA NCCL troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting.html)

**Failures/asymmetry:** a paired bidirectional rail test plus error/retry counter deltas identifies static asymmetry and some bad links. Link flap, failed-rail reroute, job recovery and convergence require controlled fault injection, and therefore belong in a separately authorized reliability test or smoke phase—not a destructive default bench. **[inference]** [rack-bench README](../../README.md#L327-L337)

**Scale:** AWS’s example is 8 GPUs on one instance; Google’s documented example is two VMs, each eight H100s, with a short all-gather; Azure H200 describes the topology and scale potential but the cited product page is not a benchmark runbook. These prove hyperscalers use small representative tests for setup and provide larger-scale context, not that an 18-tray NVL72 can be fully certified by an 8-rank run. **[observed/inference]** [AWS guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html); [Google guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/gpus/gpudirect); [Azure specs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/sizes/gpu-accelerated/nd-h200-v5-series)

## 7. Transfer to rack-bench: realistic two-hour evidence plan

The project README already specifies the right broad coverage: per-port link checks, point-to-point RDMA perftest, TCP/RDMA pair bandwidth, an intra-rack matrix sample, small-message latency, packet/error counter checks, and NCCL allreduce/allgather/alltoall from 8 B to 16 GB through MPI and `torch.distributed`, normalized bus bandwidth, plus an N-node topology-aware run. **[observed]** [rack-bench README](../../README.md#L327-L337)

A practical sequencing proposal (time is an engineering budget, not a source-prescribed provider recipe):

1. **0–10 min, gate and snapshot:** assert all expected 18 trays/ranks present; collect manifest versions, HCA/port state, topology/rail mapping, counters, NCCL env and plugin availability. Fail closed on missing rank or device; no partial-rack PASS. **[inference]** [rack-bench README](../../README.md#L327-L337)
2. **10–30 min, per-rail transport:** bidirectional short RDMA bandwidth/latency tests for each expected rail (or provider-appropriate Libfabric test), plus per-port counter snapshots. Avoid treating aggregate multi-rail bandwidth as proof each rail works. **[inference]** [NVIDIA network troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)
3. **30–45 min, sparse pair matrix:** choose topology-informed pairs (same rail, adjacent trays, cross-rack/leaf if included) to expose miswires and outliers without attempting all 153 tray pairs if that consumes the window. Preserve directed results to expose asymmetry. **[inference]** [rack-bench README](../../README.md#L327-L337)
4. **45–100 min, collective sweep:** full expected GPU ranks for a curated log-size set spanning 8 B–16 GB and allreduce/allgather/alltoall; include both MPI and `torch.distributed` paths only if both are production-supported. Archive per-size latency/algbw/busbw, selected transports, algorithm/protocol, rank map and failures. Use fixed bounded iterations and watchdogs. **[inference]** [rack-bench README](../../README.md#L327-L337); [NVIDIA nccl-tests](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests)
5. **100–115 min, loaded concurrency and counter delta:** overlap representative collectives/rail traffic only in controlled mode; sample host counters and switch/UFM telemetry if credentials exist. This can expose gross contention/ECN/PFC symptoms but is not burn-in. **[inference]** [rack-bench README](../../README.md#L327-L337)
6. **115–120 min, repeat anomalous checks and report:** classify PASS/FAIL/SKIP with raw evidence, versions and coverage; avoid turning a missing switch data source into “no congestion.” **[inference]** [rack-bench README](../../README.md#L327-L337)

Use explicit gates derived from the exact rack profile and measured baseline rather than generic “98% line rate.” Define effective aggregate rail capacity, oversubscription and expected collective scaling in the profile; store raw as well as normalized numbers. Use tolerance bands and repeat outliers. The README’s “untuned RoCE near 60%, tuned near 98%” should be treated as a motivating heuristic, not a defensible universal pass/fail threshold without topology, workload, NCCL version, and measurement-method evidence. **[inference]** [rack-bench README](../../README.md#L327-L337)

## 8. Telemetry boundary and artifacts

Minimum host-side evidence: NCCL logs (`NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` for diagnosis), per-rank command/env/version, rank-to-GPU/HCA map, NIC port link/error/retry counters before/after, RDMA test outputs, per-collective-size data, timeouts and exit codes. Include GDR path/module evidence but distinguish module presence from actual data-path use. **[inference]** [NVIDIA troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting.html); [AWS EFA guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html)

Where accessible, augment with switch-port utilization, discards, ECN marks, PFC pause counters, queue occupancy, link flaps, adaptive-routing state and SHARP job/controller evidence. Report inaccessible provider-side telemetry as a scope limitation/SKIP, not as zero errors. Host counters measure only host-observable effects; they cannot reveal every switch queue or prove fabric-wide absence of congestion. **[inference]** [NVIDIA networking troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)

## 9. Conclusions for the exact question

Hyperscalers verify GPU fabrics by executing NCCL tests across actual placed ranks and checking that the intended transport is active—not by link-rate claims alone. AWS proves EFA via Libfabric provider selection; Azure’s ND H100/H200 path is conventional ConnectX InfiniBand/GPUDirect RDMA; Google’s A3 Mega vs High/Edge paths use distinct TCPXO vs TCPX plugin stacks and different interface counts. **[observed]** [AWS guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html); [Azure H200 specs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/sizes/gpu-accelerated/nd-h200-v5-series); [Google GPUDirect guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/gpus/gpudirect)

For GB300 certification, the strongest two-hour diagnostic is layered: per-rail transport and directional checks; topology-aware pair sampling; full-rank, multi-collective NCCL sweeps with correct bus-bandwidth normalization and versioned logs; then a bounded loaded run correlated with host and switch counters. Expose coverage gaps explicitly: adaptive routing, SHARP, queue-level congestion, full-fabric scale and failure recovery need management-plane access and/or smoke tests. **[inference]** [rack-bench README](../../README.md#L327-L337); [NVIDIA troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting.html)

## Interim coverage caveats

- Public hyperscaler material is deployment-specific and does not disclose their internal acceptance thresholds, full-scale diagnostic matrices, or all switch-side telemetry/runbooks.
- The cited Azure community item is not an authoritative Microsoft runbook; official H200 specs establish topology, not a reproducible NCCL acceptance command. Public ND HNDR/H100/H200 SKU claims must be verified against the exact deployed SKU and region.
- Google’s GPUDirect page contains both TCPX and TCPXO setup, but sample images and plugin versions can change; digest/version compatibility must be verified at execution time. A3 naming does not imply all variants share an identical networking stack.
- The inspected sources do not establish portable commands/thresholds for SHARP, adaptive routing, ECN/PFC tuning, QP entropy, or a complete deprecated NCCL-variable list. Obtain the exact switch-vendor/UFM and pinned-NCCL documentation for those before implementing hard gates.
- No source examined establishes a universal busbw-to-line-rate pass percentage for GB300 NVL72. Build the denominator and thresholds from the rack’s verified topology and supplier acceptance evidence; then validate empirically.

## 10. Azure ND HNDR/H100 official evidence

Azure’s official ND H100 v5 SKU is `Standard_ND96isr_H100_v5`: 96 vCPUs, 1,900 GiB memory, eight H100 80-GB GPUs and eight network interfaces. Microsoft documents one dedicated 400-Gbps Quantum-2 ConnectX-7 InfiniBand connection per GPU, 3.2 Tb/s interconnect per VM, GPUDirect RDMA, and automatic inter-VM IB configuration between VMs in the same VM scale set. This official SKU evidence complements the H200 entry above; “HNDR”/H100 should not be conflated with H200 SKU specifics. **[observed]** [Microsoft ND H100 v5 SKU page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/nd-h100-v5-series)

Microsoft’s official Azure ML NCCL test sample describes a job that tests NCCL correctness/performance and collects standard diagnostics (including `nvcc`, `lspci`); it presents result columns including latency, `algbw`, `busbw`, and error. It is an official sample/run artifact, not a SKU-specific guaranteed performance threshold or universal bare-metal runbook. Combined with the ND H100 SKU page, the practical verification remains: launch the exact SKU group in a common VM scale set, check IB/OFED and topology, run the full-rank NCCL test, inspect transport logs and retain errors/results. **[observed/inference]** [Microsoft Learn NCCL test sample](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/samples/azure/azureml-examples/run-nccl-tests-on-gpu-to-check-performance-and-configuration); [ND H100 v5 SKU](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/nd-h100-v5-series)

## 11. Google A3 Ultra, GPUDirect RDMA, gIB and Tier_1

The A3 family is not one networking stack. Google documents A3 Ultra (`a3-ultragpu-8g`, H200) as GPUDirect RDMA over RoCE, using eight ConnectX-7 MRDMA virtual functions and 3.2 Tb/s GPU-to-GPU traffic (3.6 Tb/s listed aggregate maximum including general networking). This differs from A3 Mega (H100, TCPXO) and A3 High/Edge (H100, TCPX). Therefore the earlier “A3 stacks are TCPX/TCPXO” statement applies only to those H100 variants and must not be generalized to A3 Ultra. **[observed]** [Google GPU networking overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/gpus/gpu-network-bandwidth); [Google A3 Ultra/A4 machine types](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/accelerator-optimized-machines)

Google’s A3 Ultra/A4 create-instance instructions require two regular VPC networks for gVNIC general-purpose host communication and one RoCE-profile VPC network with eight subnets, one per CX-7 NIC; configure GPU-communication interfaces as MRDMA. This topology and transport should be audited as an RDMA fabric, not as a TCPX plugin. The official NCCL/gIB test guidance uses `NCCL_NET=gIB` and sources `/usr/local/gib/scripts/set_nccl_env.sh` (the install guide also documents the environment script); logs and prescribed gIB diagnostics are the validation path. **[observed]** [Google A3 Ultra/A4 create VM](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/gpus/create-gpu-vm-a3u-a4); [Run NCCL on GKE A4/A3 Ultra](https://docs.cloud.google.com/ai-hypercomputer/docs/nccl/test-gke-custom); [Install gIB NCCL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/ai-hypercomputer/docs/nccl/install-nccl)

Google’s documentation calls out NCCL/gIB as a Google-enhanced NCCL stack for A3 Ultra/A4, with version compatibility tables. For example, the release-notes search result lists A3 Ultra bundled NCCL 2.30.4 and minimum driver 550.90.07 for a specific diagnostic image version; that table is image-version-specific. Pin the actual gIB image digest and compatibility row for every certification run rather than recording only “latest.” **[observed/inference]** [NCCL/gIB x86 release notes](https://docs.cloud.google.com/ai-hypercomputer/docs/nccl/release-notes-x86)

**Tier_1 is a different configuration dimension.** Google’s Compute Engine Tier_1 setting (`--network-performance-configs=total-egress-bandwidth-tier=TIER_1`) selects a VM network-bandwidth performance tier for supported VM types and requires gVNIC; it does not by itself configure RoCE, attach an MRDMA interface, enable GPUDirect RDMA, guarantee an RDMA path, or prove NCCL uses one. A3 Ultra’s RDMA configuration is separately provisioned via RoCE VPC network/profile and MRDMA NICs. Report Tier_1 and RDMA provisioning as separate facts; only active NCCL/gIB transport and measured collective results verify the GPU fabric. **[observed/inference]** [Google Tier_1 configuration](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/networking/configure-vm-with-high-bandwidth-configuration); [Google GPU networking](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/gpus/gpu-network-bandwidth); [Google A3 Ultra setup](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/gpus/create-gpu-vm-a3u-a4)

## 12. RoCE GID selection: version guidance vs provider exception

NVIDIA’s networking troubleshooting page explicitly says NCCL 2.21 and later dynamically selects the GID index; for those versions `NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX` should not be set. Older NCCL versions may require identifying the RoCEv2 GID with `show_gids` and setting the corresponding index. NVIDIA NCCL 2.21 environment-variable documentation also introduces dynamic-selection filters such as `NCCL_IB_ADDR_FAMILY`, `NCCL_IB_ADDR_RANGE`, and `NCCL_IB_ROCE_VERSION_NUM`. **[observed]** [NVIDIA networking troubleshooting, page labeled NCCL 2.31.2](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html); [NCCL 2.21.5 environment variables](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2215/user-guide/docs/env.html)

This guidance conflicts with a documented, provider-specific GB300 observation: SemiAnalysis reports Google GB300’s built-in NCCL auto-selected an unroutable link-local GID and hung, while setting `NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX=3` fixed that tested setup. That finding does not invalidate NCCL’s general 2.21+ default guidance and does not justify forcing index 3 on all RoCE fabrics. Treat forced GID as a pinned provider/image/NCCL-specific workaround: first capture version, `show_gids`, route/address state and logs; test default selection; only then apply documented provider exception and record it in the certification profile. **[observed/inference]** [SemiAnalysis ClusterMAX 3.0](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard); [NVIDIA networking troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)

## 13. Precise local evidence references

Rack-bench’s local network benchmark contract is in [README.md](../../README.md#L327-L337), lines 327–337: perftest, pair bandwidth, latency/counters, collective sweep, normalization, and N-node run. Its network inventory and NCCL/GDR/topology audit contract is in [README.md](../../README.md#L170-L241), lines 170–241. The README states planned checks; it is a local design spec, not independent evidence that tests are implemented. **[observed]** [Local README](../../README.md#L327-L337)

- EFA is SRD-based and supports extended verbs, but whether `perftest` can exercise the intended EFA mode depends on the installed build/provider and command support. Avoid asserting conventional RC `ib_write_bw` options work; verify `--help`, provider support, and AWS-specific instructions on the target image.

## 14. A4X Max / GB300 directly relevant comparison

Google documents A4X Max with GB300 Ultra Superchips as an 18-instance, 72-GPU NVLink subblock; scale-out RoCE networking connects those subblocks. Its network design has four 800-Gbps ConnectX-8 NICs presented as eight physical functions (PFs), with two 400-Gbps rails per NIC. These are published topology and bandwidth specifications, not measured throughput or proof that any deployed rack achieves line rate. The architecture is useful comparison evidence for GB300-class rack scale, but it is not evidence that a rack-bench installation has matching cabling, routing, balance, or NCCL performance. **[observed/inference]** [Google GPU networking and monitoring](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/gpus/gpu-network-bandwidth)

For observability, Google warns that the `_phy` counters on A3 Ultra/A4 MRDMA virtual functions are visible but do not update; use vPort counters for those VFs. A4X Max uses PFs, which expose physical counters. Thus counter names/interface presence alone are not telemetry validation: rack-bench should verify counter movement during traffic, label the counter layer (VF/vPort vs PF/physical), and avoid interpreting static `_phy` values as zero traffic or healthy links. **[observed/inference]** [Google GPU networking and monitoring](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/gpus/gpu-network-bandwidth)

The later addenda in §§10–14 extend and supersede the earlier narrower Azure and Google A3 coverage in §§2 and 9: specifically, ND H100/HNDR evidence supplements H200; A3 Ultra is GPUDirect RDMA/RoCE/gIB rather than TCPX/TCPXO; and A4X Max provides the directly relevant GB300-scale comparator. **[observed]** [Azure ND H100 SKU](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/nd-h100-v5-series); [Google GPU networking and monitoring](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/gpus/gpu-network-bandwidth)

## Gaps

- Azure official sources establish ND H100/H200 topology and an official NCCL sample, but the reviewed source set did not provide a single authoritative, current ND HNDR end-to-end fabric troubleshooting runbook with acceptance thresholds and counter interpretation.
- Google documentation distinguishes A3 Ultra RoCE/MRDMA/gIB from H100 TCPX/TCPXO and Tier_1, but exact installed hardware/firmware diagnostics and provider-side switch telemetry remain deployment-dependent.
- EFA is SRD-based and supports extended verbs, but whether `perftest` can exercise the intended EFA mode depends on the installed build/provider and command support. Avoid asserting conventional RC `ib_write_bw` options work; verify `--help`, provider support, and AWS-specific instructions on the target image.
