# N04 — Large-company fabric mechanisms and rack diagnostics

Research date: 2026-10-11. All claims below carry a source URL.

Claims are marked **[observed]** (explicit in a source), **[calculated]** (arithmetic from stated inputs), or **[inference]** (recommendation or interpretation). This brief addresses only east-west fabric quality; it excludes north-south internet and storage.

## 1. Answer in brief

A two-hour rack test cannot certify hyperscale-fabric architecture. It can expose the same *failure signatures* large operators describe: low path/rail entropy and imbalance, congestion and pause propagation, topology or link faults, and collective stragglers. Run repeatable NCCL collectives on the GB300 target (RCCL results are comparator evidence only) alongside per-rail RDMA measurements, capture counters before/after, and compare rail/link symmetry and latency tails. **[inference]** These tests diagnose the rack and its currently reachable fabric; they cannot prove global scale, routing control-plane quality, or provider-wide topology without operator telemetry ([Meta production observability](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3651890.3672233); [Google Jupiter](https://research.google/pubs/jupiter-evolving-transforming-googles-datacenter-network-via-optical-circuit-switches-and-software-defined-networking)).

The evidence separates into: production mechanisms and observed failures (§2); research/announced transport designs (§3); tenant-visible measurements and provider-side evidence (§4–5). Swift is Google-authored, not Meta-authored ([Google Research, Swift](https://research.google/pubs/swift-delay-is-simple-and-effective-for-congestion-control-in-the-datacenter)). Microsoft Sirius is a prototype/simulation result, not evidence of production deployment ([Microsoft Research, Sirius](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/video/sirius-a-flat-datacenter-network-with-nanosecond-optical-switching-sigcomm-2020-short-talk)). **[observed]**

## 2. Production mechanisms and failure explanations

### 2.1 Meta: RoCE performance is an end-to-end property, not a NIC line-rate property **[observed]**

Meta describes dedicated frontend and backend fabrics; the backend connects RDMA NICs and carries distributed training. Its production AI zone uses a two-stage Clos and, for larger domains, an aggregator layer; cross-zone traffic is intentionally oversubscribed and ECMP-balanced. A topology-aware scheduler limits cross-zone traffic by placing ranks across zones with a minimum-cut heuristic ([Meta Engineering, 2024](https://engineering.fb.com/2024/08/05/data-center-engineering/roce-network-distributed-ai-training-at-scale/)).

The operationally useful failure mechanisms are concrete:

1. **Low entropy + ECMP hash collisions.** AI collectives can have few, repetitive flows, bursty at millisecond scale, with elephant flows at NIC rate. Five-tuple ECMP then fails to spread load evenly. **[observed]** This means aggregate link capacity can look healthy while one path/rail is congested and a collective slows ([Meta Engineering, 2024](https://engineering.fb.com/2024/08/05/data-center-engineering/roce-network-distributed-ai-training-at-scale/)).
2. **Placement-induced uplink imbalance.** Meta reports partial rack allocation caused uneven uplink use; training performance degraded by >30%. **[observed]** Test directional/rank-to-rank performance and per-rail symmetry, rather than just total bandwidth ([Meta Engineering, 2024](https://engineering.fb.com/2024/08/05/data-center-engineering/roce-network-distributed-ai-training-at-scale/)).
3. **Failure remapping can create secondary congestion.** A failed uplink or switch caused ECMP reassignment that collided with existing flows and slowed the whole job. **[observed]** Baseline and one-link-degraded tests, if safely supported, can reveal lack of path headroom; provider switch/link event telemetry is needed to attribute remapping ([Meta Engineering, 2024](https://engineering.fb.com/2024/08/05/data-center-engineering/roce-network-distributed-ai-training-at-scale/)).
4. **More QPs/entropy may help, but is not a universal fix.** Meta reports enhanced ECMP hashing on destination QP plus QP scaling improved AllReduce up to 40%; it also notes probabilistic hashing and workload-specific tuning remain limitations. **[observed]** For certification, record NCCL channel/QP configuration and compare single-/multi-rail results; do not mandate Meta’s private routing design ([Meta Engineering, 2024](https://engineering.fb.com/2024/08/05/data-center-engineering/roce-network-distributed-ai-training-at-scale/)).
5. **Congestion control and PFC behavior are workload- and implementation-dependent.** Meta reports DCQCN tuning degraded at 400G due in part to firmware behavior/visibility; its production setup later ran over a year with PFC and without transport-level congestion control, reporting stable AI collectives, while acknowledging dependence on coordination with collective software and relative GPU/network throughput. **[observed]** This conflicts with simplistic rules that every RoCE fabric must show a particular DCQCN/PFC profile. Measure outcomes and counters; don't prescribe a provider architecture ([Meta Engineering, 2024](https://engineering.fb.com/2024/08/05/data-center-engineering/roce-network-distributed-ai-training-at-scale/)).

The paper's transferable lesson is instrumentation across **fabric, routing, transport, and collectives**, because any layer can explain slow jobs ([SIGCOMM 2024 paper](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3651890.3672233)). **[inference]** Tenant-visible NCCL timing alone flags the symptom; counters and operator data are needed for root cause.

### 2.2 Google: Swift is Google's congestion control, not Meta's **[observed]**

Swift is a Google datacenter transport using hardware timestamps, accurate RTT, AIMD and pacing under extreme congestion; its authors report production deployment and testbed results including 100 Gb/s/server near full load with low short-RPC tail latency ([Google Research, Swift](https://research.google/pubs/swift-delay-is-simple-and-effective-for-congestion-control-in-the-datacenter)). The primary source identifies Google authors and explicitly says deployment in Google datacenters. **[observed]** Do not attribute Swift to Meta.

Diagnostic implication: latency inflation under load can indicate queues/congestion even when no packets drop. **[inference]** Capture unloaded baseline latency and loaded latency during concurrent collective/RDMA traffic; report median and tail, not just peak throughput. Swift itself is not a tenant-side test and its results do not imply that a GB300 rack uses Swift.

### 2.3 Google Jupiter: production topology engineering, not rack-level optical tuning **[observed]**

Google reports a decade of Jupiter production experience serving live traffic. The evolution uses MEMS optical circuit switches for dynamic topology reconfiguration, centralized SDN traffic engineering, and automated operations; reported outcomes include 5× speed/capacity, 30% lower capex, 41% lower power, and throughput comparable to Clos for production traffic patterns ([Google Research, Jupiter Evolving, SIGCOMM 2022](https://research.google/pubs/jupiter-evolving-transforming-googles-datacenter-network-via-optical-circuit-switches-and-software-defined-networking)).

This demonstrates that topology can change under software control and that routing/traffic engineering is part of fabric performance. **[inference]** A two-hour tenant test should detect unexpected asymmetry, path-dependent throughput, or transient collective regressions, but cannot observe or certify OCS schedules or SDN policy without provider telemetry. Do not infer that the Chennai rack has optical circuit switching.

## 3. Research and emerging mechanisms — not blanket production claims

### 3.1 MetaRoCE: emerging transport specification and validation results **[observed]**

Meta's August 2026 post describes MetaRoCE as a new RDMA transport designed for AI-scale Ethernet and says it is releasing a specification, reference implementation, and compliance suite through OCP. Its design uses per-path RTT/ECN/utilization, packet spraying, explicit loss recovery, and per-path congestion state; it does not require PFC or switch-side spraying ([Meta Engineering, MetaRoCE](https://engineering.fb.com/2026/08/24/networking-traffic/metaroce-rdma-transport-ai-ethernet)).

The post reports a 64-node AMD GPU cluster RCCL comparison and simulations/validations including loss and plane-failure experiments. It reports graceful recovery and throughput at packet loss, but these are Meta-reported results, not independent GB300 certification evidence. **[observed]** The post says the OCP release is planned for October 2026; research date is October 11, so release completion should not be assumed ([same source](https://engineering.fb.com/2026/08/24/networking-traffic/metaroce-rdma-transport-ai-ethernet)).

Transferable diagnostic ideas: per-path telemetry, distinguish congestion from path failure, and test behavior when one path/plane is degraded. **[inference]** For rack-bench, these are counter/request fields to obtain from a compatible NIC/provider, not a reason to install MetaRoCE or alter rack configuration.

### 3.2 Microsoft Sirius: optical switching prototype plus simulation **[observed]**

Microsoft Research describes Sirius as a proposed optically switched flat datacenter network with nanosecond-scale reconfiguration, routing/scheduling co-design, congestion control, and time synchronization. It reports a small custom-laser prototype demonstrating 3.84 ns end-to-end reconfiguration over 50 Gb/s channels, and large-scale simulations estimating 74–77% lower power than an ideal electrical nonblocking network ([Microsoft Research, Sirius](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/video/sirius-a-flat-datacenter-network-with-nanosecond-optical-switching-sigcomm-2020-short-talk)).

This is research evidence, not a claim that Microsoft deployed Sirius in production or that a commercial GB300 rack uses it. **[inference]** The transferable point is only that topology, scheduling, and congestion control can interact; rack-bench should assess measured path behavior, not make speculative optical hardware changes.

## 4. Tenant-visible checks feasible inside two hours

| Check | Failure signal it can expose | Practical method and boundary |
|---|---|---|
| **Per-rail RDMA bandwidth and latency** | Dead/slow rail, asymmetric paths, link-rate mismatch | Run `ib_write_bw` and `ib_write_lat` per HCA/rail and direction; record throughput, latency, link state/rate, and RDMA error-counter deltas. NVIDIA recommends host- and GPU-memory comparisons for GPUDirect RDMA. **[inference]** Use supported local build options ([NVIDIA NCCL networking troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html). |
| **NCCL size sweep, 8 B–16 GB** | Small-message latency floor, bandwidth plateau, protocol transition, rank straggler | Run repeated all-reduce (and all-to-all if available) over the prescribed sizes; capture algorithm/protocol/channels and per-rank results (use RCCL only as comparator evidence, not as the GB300 target test). Compare against declared hardware/link envelope, not an unsupported universal threshold. **[inference]** See [NVIDIA NCCL performance and tuning](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/performance_and_tuning.html) and [NVIDIA nccl-tests](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests) for primary tooling guidance. |
| **Symmetry and repeatability** | ECMP/QP entropy problems, one slow path, instability | Compare each rail, both directions, and repeat runs; report min/median/p95 or max-rank completion time plus normalized goodput. Aggregate GB/s can conceal a slow rank. **[inference]** Meta's reported low-entropy collision and >30% placement penalty motivate this check ([Meta Engineering](https://engineering.fb.com/2024/08/05/data-center-engineering/roce-network-distributed-ai-training-at-scale/)). |
| **Concurrent load / latency under load** | Queue buildup, incast, PFC pause, transport instability | Overlap collective traffic with per-rail probes where supported; record latency inflation, throughput loss, retries, ECN/CNP and pause counters. **[inference]** Do not treat absence of PFC as a universal pass condition; Meta's production experience shows operating models differ ([Meta Engineering](https://engineering.fb.com/2024/08/05/data-center-engineering/roce-network-distributed-ai-training-at-scale/)). |
| **Controlled link/rail degradation** | Poor failover, asymmetric rerouting, collective collapse | Only with provider approval: disable/isolate one rail or use documented maintenance/fault injection, then compare collective goodput and recovery. Never administratively alter shared fabric unilaterally. **[inference]** Meta documents link/switch failures and path reassignment as a source of collective slowdown; without approved injection, compare observed events and provider counters ([Meta Engineering](https://engineering.fb.com/2024/08/05/data-center-engineering/roce-network-distributed-ai-training-at-scale/)). |
| **SHARP / in-network collective path** | Missing/offline SHARP, fallback behavior, unexpected performance | Record whether SHARP is supported and actually selected; compare same collective with/without it only when supported and safe. **[inference]** Feature availability alone is not measured performance. NVIDIA documents SHARP offload integration with NCCL and configuration requirements ([NVIDIA SHARP documentation](https://docs.nvidia.com/networking/display/sharpumv352/nvidia+scalable+hierarchical+aggregation+and+reduction+protocol)). |

**Two-hour allocation [inference]:** reserve ~10 min for inventory/counters and environment capture; ~25 min for per-rail RDMA baseline; ~50 min for NCCL size sweeps and repeats; ~20 min for concurrent-load/latency checks; ~10 min for optional SHARP comparison or approved degradation; ~5 min for final counter capture and report. Keep buffer for setup and one rerun. No long burn-in, fleet-scale all-to-all, or disruptive fault injection fits reliably in this window.

The excerpted local project context is in `/home/avirus/.herdr/worktrees/rack-bench/research-network/.lavish/network-research/README.md` (research boundaries and acceptance) and `research.md` (N04 scope and expected evidence). These are context documents, not benchmark implementations or evidence of local test behavior. **[observed]**

## 5. Counters, root-cause limits, and evidence confidence

### 5.1 Collect before/after deltas, not just snapshots **[inference]**

Capture per-port bytes, errors/discards, link state, symbol/CRC faults, retransmits/timeouts where exposed, ECN marks/CNPs for RoCE, PFC pause frames/duration per priority, and NIC queue/congestion counters. Timestamp alongside NCCL run IDs, ranks, rail mapping, and test phases. Counter names and semantics vary by NIC/switch generation; record device/driver/firmware and units. A static counter value without a delta or run correlation is weak evidence. NVIDIA identifies RDMA retry/error, InfiniBand port-error, and RoCE drop/pause/ECN/CNP counters as diagnostics ([NVIDIA NCCL networking troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)).

### 5.2 Provider telemetry required for root cause **[inference]**

Tenant data can show *where* performance is uneven but usually not *why*. Request time-correlated switch port counters and queue occupancy, ECN/PFC and pause propagation, ECMP route/hash or adaptive-routing decisions, link flaps/optic alarms, switch health, oversubscription/topology mapping, and maintenance/fault events. Meta's account explicitly spans fabric, routing, transport and collectives; Google's Jupiter relies on centralized SDN and automated topology operations ([Meta paper](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3651890.3672233); [Google Jupiter](https://research.google/pubs/jupiter-evolving-transforming-googles-datacenter-network-via-optical-circuit-switches-and-software-defined-networking)). **[inference]** Without such evidence, report “measured symptom; cause unconfirmed,” not “bad ECMP” or “bad PFC.”

### 5.3 Conflicts and confidence

- **PFC/DCQCN expectations:** Meta's production account reports stable AI traffic without transport congestion control after DCQCN issues, while that account is workload/topology specific. **[observed]** Confidence high for the account, low for generalizing it to another vendor/rack ([Meta Engineering](https://engineering.fb.com/2024/08/05/data-center-engineering/roce-network-distributed-ai-training-at-scale/)). Score measured loss, latency, pauses and goodput; do not score a configuration dogma.
- **Adaptive routing/QP scaling:** Meta documents its own evolution and gains, but results depend on traffic, placement and switch/NIC capabilities. **[observed]** Confidence high as an explanation of possible failure modes; not a universal expected feature ([Meta Engineering](https://engineering.fb.com/2024/08/05/data-center-engineering/roce-network-distributed-ai-training-at-scale/)).
- **Swift:** Google production deployment is directly stated by Google Research; it is not evidence of adoption by Meta or this rack. **[observed]** High confidence in authorship and reported deployment ([Google Research, Swift](https://research.google/pubs/swift-delay-is-simple-and-effective-for-congestion-control-in-the-datacenter)).
- **Jupiter:** Google primary publication explicitly says production experience on live traffic. **[observed]** High confidence in production status; low relevance as a rack configuration prescription ([Google Research, Jupiter](https://research.google/pubs/jupiter-evolving-transforming-googles-datacenter-network-via-optical-circuit-switches-and-software-defined-networking)).
- **Sirius:** Microsoft Research source explicitly distinguishes prototype and simulation. **[observed]** High confidence in reported experimental status; it does not establish production deployment ([Microsoft Research, Sirius](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/video/sirius-a-flat-datacenter-network-with-nanosecond-optical-switching-sigcomm-2020-short-talk)).
- **MetaRoCE:** Meta source reports open specification plans and a vendor implementation/testing; it does not establish broad production availability or GB300 compatibility. **[observed]** High confidence in what Meta claims, lower confidence in independent/generalizable performance ([Meta Engineering, MetaRoCE](https://engineering.fb.com/2026/08/24/networking-traffic/metaroce-rdma-transport-ai-ethernet)).

## 6. Gaps

- No public primary source establishes which transport, adaptive-routing mechanism, SHARP configuration, or congestion-control policy is present in the target Chennai rack. Obtain operator inventory and configuration evidence.
- Public large-company accounts are not independent evaluations; performance numbers and causal interpretations are operator-reported. Independent replication on the target 18-tray rack is required.
- No defensible universal goodput/latency pass thresholds can be set from these sources alone. Thresholds require GB300/NVL72 topology, NIC speed, rail count, software versions, and vendor acceptance envelope.
- Per-rail fault injection and simultaneous congestion testing may be unsafe or unavailable to tenants. If unavailable, provider-side counters and event timelines are necessary; otherwise certify observed performance only.
- MetaRoCE's announced October 2026 release may post-date the research date label or remain pending; no claim is made that the specification/release is already available.
- The seed phrase “self-serving fabric” did not yield an identifiable primary-source title in a bounded exact-phrase search; this is a search gap, not evidence that no such post exists.
- The local files cited above are scope/context only. No repository source files or exact line-level implementation evidence were provided or inspected for this N04 task.

# Neocloud fabric evidence for a two-hour GB300 rack certification

Research date: 2026-10-11. All claims below carry a source URL.

## 1. Scope and evidence standard

### 1.1 What counts as tenant-obtainable evidence

[observed] This brief concerns east-west GPU fabric evidence that a tenant can access or reproduce: configuration and topology disclosures, executable benchmark recipes, measured collective results, and health telemetry. Vendor link-rate claims are not measured tenant results. The user-provided bench contract requires measured (never vendor-claimed) PASS outcomes. Separately, README specifies quick checks including port/link state, perftest, TCP/RDMA pairs, a sampled intra-rack matrix, small-message latency, loss counters, and NCCL allreduce/allgather/alltoall from 8 B to 16 GB; it reports algbw/busbw as line-rate percentages and checks curve monotonicity. [README network checks](../../README.md#L327-L337); [network audit fields](../../README.md#L170-L184)

[observed] The intended separation is audit inventory/configuration first, active QP creation and a two-rank all-reduce canary during bench. Audit captures rail names/planes, NCCL variables/plugins, and accessible switch information; switch access is optional and unavailable switches are SKIP, with host RDMA counters as fallback. [README NCCL configuration and active validation](../../README.md#L220-L241); [network audit fields](../../README.md#L170-L184)

## 2. Provider evidence: claims, recipes, and disclosure

### 2.1 Nebius: bandwidth and Quantum-X800 are published capabilities, not pass results

[observed] Nebius documentation states that each GPU NIC provides 400 Gbps and an 8-GPU VM totals 3.2 Tbps, with GPUDirect RDMA. It describes clusters as occupying physical InfiniBand fabrics and uses unique P-Keys to isolate tenant clusters on shared physical fabric. These are architecture/capability statements; the documentation does not provide per-rail measured bandwidth, latency, goodput, or a GB300 tenant result. [Nebius GPU cluster networking](https://docs.nebius.com/compute/clusters/gpu)

[observed] Nebius AI Cloud 3.1 marketing announces GB300 NVL72 and HGX B300 on 800 Gbps NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand and characterizes this as doubling throughput for distributed workloads. This establishes a product/fabric deployment claim, not measured NCCL output or proof every rail achieves line rate. [Nebius announcement](https://nebius.com/newsroom/nebius-ai-cloud-3-1-delivers-next-generation-nvidia-blackwell-ultra-compute-with-transparent-capacity-management-for-ai-at-scale)

[observed] Nebius does publish a tenant-usable NCCL test route: its GPU-cluster guide points to an MPIrun tutorial using NCCL tests, and to an Soperator all-reduce example; a physical-state test is separately linked. That is actionable test guidance, but a recipe is not a published fleet baseline. [Nebius guide](https://docs.nebius.com/compute/clusters/gpu); [Soperator all-reduce example](https://docs.nebius.com/slurm-soperator/jobs/examples/nccl-all-reduce)

### 2.2 CoreWeave: strongest public NCCL troubleshooting and topology-health evidence

[observed] CoreWeave publishes `nccl-tests` container images and MPI/Slurm sample jobs, plus a baseline-driven triage method: record `busbw` from a small known-good group, then compare suspect nodes against that baseline. Their guide distinguishes single-node success (NVLink path) from multi-node failure (RDMA path), and notes TCP fallback can explain very low multi-node throughput. [CoreWeave nccl-tests](https://github.com/coreweave/nccl-tests); [NCCL error triage](https://docs.coreweave.com/support/sunk/articles/what-do-nccl-errors-mean); [InfiniBand GPUDirect RDMA guide](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/networking/hpc-interconnect/use-gpudirect-rdma)

[observed] CoreWeave's GB300 RoCE guidance explicitly distinguishes NCCL's verbs path from UCX-based traffic: NCCL passing does not prove UCX/NIXL works. It provides RoCE-specific variables and recommends UCX perftest for UCX workloads. This supports testing the actual transport stack in addition to NCCL. [CoreWeave RoCE GPUDirect guide](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/networking/hpc-interconnect/use-gpudirect-rdma-roce)

[observed] CoreWeave describes a rail-optimized design with large rail pods, fewer hops for communicating GPUs, and internal tools that monitor link flaps and bit errors in context of rail group/SuperPOD/fabric impact. This is a first-party architecture/operations disclosure, not tenant-accessible raw per-rail results or flap-rate time series. [CoreWeave engineering statement](https://www.coreweave.com/blog/coreweave-ranks-as-1-ai-cloud-backed-by-semianalysiss-platinum-clustermax-tm-rating)

[observed] A CoreWeave sample intentionally disables CollNet/SHARP (`NCCL_COLLNET_ENABLE=0`) for a non-SHARP reference run. This is useful experimentally: compare identical runs with SHARP disabled/enabled only where tenant permissions and fabric support allow, and do not attribute a gain to the raw link rate. [CoreWeave SGLang/NCCL test example](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/cks/clusters/frameworks/sglang)

### 2.3 Lambda: dedicated fabric disclosure, limited public performance evidence

[observed] Lambda Private Cloud documents a dedicated tenant network design: in-band Ethernet plus InfiniBand, compute nodes on a spine-leaf IB fabric, and unrestricted compute-to-compute communication. It says RoCE may substitute for IB depending on cluster size. The document describes topology/isolation, not per-rail measurements or workload benchmark results. [Lambda security posture](https://docs.lambda.ai/private-cloud/security-posture)

[observed] Lambda's managed Slurm health-check material says network checks confirm high-speed fabric links are present, up, and at full speed, and points to diagnostics/benchmark jobs in `/data/examples`. This is evidence of a provider-side health-check practice, but the public wording supplies no numerical thresholds, per-rail output, or time-series fault rates. [Lambda Managed Slurm health checks](https://docs.lambda.ai/managed-slurm/health-checks)

[observed] Lambda's SHARP article explains tenant-facing use through NCCL-aware collectives when the Quantum InfiniBand network and plugin are configured. It is enablement guidance, not a comparative measured result. [Lambda SHARP guide](https://lambda.ai/blog/nvidia-sharp-on-lambda-1cc)

### 2.4 Crusoe: unusually concrete configuration disclosure, no public per-rail results

[observed] Crusoe lists 8 HCAs and aggregate 3.2 Tbps for documented H100/H200 SXM instances (1.6 Tbps A100), and exposes logical IB networks and partitions for tenant placement/isolation. The figures are advertised instance capacity, not measured goodput. [Crusoe IB management](https://docs.crusoecloud.com/networking/infiniband/managing-infiniband-networks)

[observed] Crusoe supplies NCCL topology XML files by instance type and requires topology/configuration handling for virtualized PCI addresses; its image service sets `NCCL_TOPO_FILE`, and the guidance excludes an Ethernet HCA from `NCCL_IB_HCA`. This is strong configuration guidance and a concrete warning that incorrect device/topology selection can invalidate collective results. [Crusoe IB management](https://docs.crusoecloud.com/networking/infiniband/managing-infiniband-networks)

[observed] Crusoe's burn-in description says multi-node NCCL collectives test the IB fabric and contrasts this with single-node GPU P2P/NVLink tests for fault attribution. It describes the test class but does not publish rail-separated measured tables or flap rates. [Crusoe burn-in overview](https://www.crusoe.ai/resources/blog/how-crusoe-burn-in-tests-every-node-before-it-reaches-you)

## 3. Routing, SHARP, and what aggregate NCCL can hide

### 3.1 Rail-optimized versus static routing

[observed] CoreWeave publicly describes rail-optimized topology and fewer hops, but the cited disclosure does not establish that tenants can choose or inspect adaptive routing policy. [CoreWeave statement](https://www.coreweave.com/blog/coreweave-ranks-as-1-ai-cloud-backed-by-semianalysiss-platinum-clustermax-tm-rating)

[observed] NVIDIA's Quantum InfiniBand operations guidance recommends validating topology and fabric health and reviewing link monitoring/telemetry; this is operational guidance, not evidence that any named neocloud exposes tenant controls for adaptive routing. [NVIDIA Quantum InfiniBand operations](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/simplifying-network-operations-for-ai-with-nvidia-quantum-infiniband)

[inference] A two-hour tenant certification should not attempt to infer routing policy from aggregate NCCL alone. Capture HCA-to-rail mapping and per-port link state, then compare rail-isolated point-to-point and collective runs where controls permit. If the provider does not expose route mode or rail pinning, record that as unobservable rather than asserting adaptive/static behavior. This follows README’s per-rail topology and validation requirements ([README](../../README.md#L170-L184), [NCCL configuration](../../README.md#L220-L237)); NVIDIA recommends topology and fabric-health validation but does not establish tenant routing controls ([operations guidance](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/simplifying-network-operations-for-ai-with-nvidia-quantum-infiniband)).

### 3.2 SHARP: separate feature validation from baseline

[observed] NVIDIA describes SHARP as switch-offloaded collective reduction integrated with NCCL, intended to reduce host/network work and improve scalability; these are mechanism and benefit claims, not a guaranteed gain for every workload. [NVIDIA SHARP overview](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/advancing-performance-with-nvidia-sharp-in-network-computing)

[observed] Nebius Quantum-X800 material advertises SHARP-capable fabric context, while Lambda gives SHARP enablement guidance and CoreWeave offers a non-SHARP NCCL reference configuration. Public sources reviewed here do not provide comparable tenant-measured SHARP-on versus SHARP-off numbers for GB300. [Nebius announcement](https://nebius.com/newsroom/nebius-ai-cloud-3-1-delivers-next-generation-nvidia-blackwell-ultra-compute-with-transparent-capacity-management-for-ai-at-scale); [Lambda SHARP guide](https://lambda.ai/blog/nvidia-sharp-on-lambda-1cc); [CoreWeave sample](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/cks/clusters/frameworks/sglang)

[inference] In the certification window, first establish a non-SHARP known-good collective baseline, then run a short identical SHARP-enabled comparison if plugin/fabric access is available. Record actual plugin selection and logs; a configuration flag alone does not prove offload occurred. Keep SHARP as an optimization/feature check, not a substitute for ordinary per-rail correctness and bandwidth.

## 4. Recommended two-hour evidence plan

### 4.1 Fast checks that fit and diagnose

[inference] A practical order is: (1) inventory each port/HCA, negotiated speed/state, rail mapping, and accessible counters; (2) run one short `ib_write_bw` and `ib_read_bw` per rail in both directions, recording achieved throughput and errors; (3) test a small set of node pairs including same-rack and cross-rack/scale-out endpoints; (4) run NCCL all-reduce/all-gather/all-to-all at representative sizes including tiny latency-sensitive messages, medium messages, and large transfers; (5) compute goodput against the correct aggregate or per-rail line-rate denominator; (6) inspect monotonicity and asymmetry, then repeat suspect points. This aligns with the local README contract. [README network bench checks](../../README.md#L327-L337)

[inference] Prioritize the 8 B–16 GB sweep in a bounded set rather than exhaustive dense sampling: include 8 B/latency, logarithmically spaced transitions, and large payloads; run MPI and `torch.distributed` canaries only as time allows. Compare collective `algbw` and `busbw` to distinguish algorithm-level operation throughput from fabric-equivalent bandwidth; retain raw output and environment/configuration for reproducibility. [README network bench checks](../../README.md#L327-L337)

[inference] For RoCE, gather ECN/PFC and congestion-control configuration plus port counters before and after load; for IB gather port symbol/link errors and available congestion/fabric counters. A clean zero-loss counter is meaningful only if counters are readable and the measurement interval is captured. Dead rail = absent/down HCA or failed QP; slow rail = per-rail goodput materially below matched peers; asymmetry = directional read/write or endpoint differences. Use profile thresholds, not vendor claims. README calls for ECN configuration, packet-loss checks, and RDMA counter fallback ([network audit](../../README.md#L170-L184), [network bench](../../README.md#L327-L337)); NVIDIA also recommends telemetry review ([guidance](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/simplifying-network-operations-for-ai-with-nvidia-quantum-infiniband)).

### 4.2 Scale-out and telemetry evidence

[observed] Keep one physical plane distinct from one logical HCA rail: these labels describe different levels of topology and do not alone prove independent path diversity. README explicitly distinguishes planes and expected HCA names ([README](../../README.md#L222-L225)); Crusoe also supplies topology/configuration artifacts ([guide](https://docs.crusoecloud.com/networking/infiniband/managing-infiniband-networks)).

[observed] CoreWeave exposes internal monitoring for link flaps and bit errors, but the public source does not show tenant access to raw telemetry or historical flap rates. Lambda describes provider management/observability nodes; it does not specify tenant-facing IB telemetry fields. Nebius documents diagnostic logs including GPU/InfiniBand/node logs in its changelog, but cited docs do not supply continuous per-rail telemetry guarantees. [CoreWeave statement](https://www.coreweave.com/blog/coreweave-ranks-as-1-ai-cloud-backed-by-semianalysiss-platinum-clustermax-tm-rating); [Lambda posture](https://docs.lambda.ai/private-cloud/security-posture); [Nebius changelog](https://docs.nebius.com/changelog)

[inference] Within two hours, snapshot counters before/after traffic and preserve node/port identifiers, link transitions if exposed, NCCL logs, and timestamps; README permits host RDMA counters as fallback ([README](../../README.md#L181-L184)). A snapshot cannot establish long-term flap rates. Importantly, multi-node traffic within an NVL72/MNNVL scale-up domain may still use NVLink rather than RDMA: prove RDMA via NCCL logs and counters, or use a cross-rack peer. README warns jobs must not silently cross the NVLink domain ([README](../../README.md#L232-L237)); CoreWeave distinguishes NVLink and RDMA paths ([triage guide](https://docs.coreweave.com/support/sunk/articles/what-do-nccl-errors-mean)).

## 5. Measured results versus disclosed claims

### 5.1 Measured tenant-visible performance

[observed] Among the primary provider materials cited above, the evidence found is chiefly testing instructions, topology/configuration guidance, or operational descriptions. The cited Nebius 3.2 Tbps and Quantum-X800 figures, Crusoe 3.2 Tbps figures, and CoreWeave rail-optimized description are not tenant-measured per-rail results. CoreWeave's baseline method tells customers how to compare their own `busbw`, but does not publish a universal threshold. [Nebius](https://docs.nebius.com/compute/clusters/gpu); [Crusoe](https://docs.crusoecloud.com/networking/infiniband/managing-infiniband-networks); [CoreWeave triage](https://docs.coreweave.com/support/sunk/articles/what-do-nccl-errors-mean)

### 5.2 Missing disclosure, carefully scoped

[observed] In the reviewed primary public pages for Nebius, CoreWeave, Lambda, and Crusoe, I did not find comparable per-rail measured `ib_write_bw`/`ib_read_bw` tables, directional asymmetry results, rail-level goodput percentages, or quantified flap rates. This bounded finding applies to the cited public sources, not private portals or internal data: [Nebius fabric/NCCL guide](https://docs.nebius.com/compute/clusters/gpu), [CoreWeave NCCL triage](https://docs.coreweave.com/support/sunk/articles/what-do-nccl-errors-mean) and [rail disclosure](https://www.coreweave.com/blog/coreweave-ranks-as-1-ai-cloud-backed-by-semianalysiss-platinum-clustermax-tm-rating), [Lambda posture](https://docs.lambda.ai/private-cloud/security-posture) and [health checks](https://docs.lambda.ai/managed-slurm/health-checks), [Crusoe IB guide](https://docs.crusoecloud.com/networking/infiniband/managing-infiniband-networks).

[observed] Provider evidence differs: Nebius publishes capacity and an NCCL recipe; CoreWeave publishes sample images, baselining/triage, and qualitative rail-aware operations; Lambda publishes private-cluster topology and link health-check descriptions; Crusoe publishes per-instance bandwidth claims, tenant partitioning, and NCCL topology/configuration artifacts. None of those evidence classes should be conflated with a rack-bench PASS.

## 6. Gaps

1. [observed] Public material reviewed does not settle whether Nebius exposes per-rail telemetry, adaptive-routing controls, tenant-visible ECN/PFC counters, or measured GB300 collective baselines. Obtain a tenant cluster and inspect available logs/counters; request a rail-separated result set.
2. [observed] CoreWeave's public rail/flap disclosure is qualitative. The public pages reviewed do not establish tenant access to flap histories, rail-level counters, or routing mode. Ask for anonymized telemetry export and run the baseline recipe on the target allocation.
3. [observed] Lambda's public private-cloud description states dedicated spine-leaf IB and health checks but supplies no per-rail measured output; availability of `/data/examples` and management telemetry may depend on deployment. Verify with a real handoff.
4. [observed] Crusoe's published detailed topology files and bandwidth table cover A100/H100/H200 examples, not GB300. Do not extrapolate those advertised capabilities to GB300 or Quantum-X800.
5. [inference] Public evidence is insufficient to set universal pass thresholds for 8 B–16 GB NCCL curves or SHARP uplift. Use the rack certification profile, matched topology, and measured hardware line rate; report capability claims separately.

# N02 — Accepted hyperscaler evidence

Research date: 2026-10-11.

Full returned brief: [hyperscalers.md](../hyperscalers.md).
Question: How do hyperscalers verify and diagnose GPU fabrics?
State: done. The state describes research acceptance, not fabric PASS.

- [observed] AWS EFA uses aws-ofi-nccl and Libfabric EFA; its guide supplies provider logs and a launch command (§2.1).
- [observed] Azure ND H100/H200 describes dedicated InfiniBand/GDR; an official NCCL sample supplies test output (§2.2, §10).
- [observed] A3 High/Edge uses TCPX; Mega uses TCPXO; Ultra uses RoCE/MRDMA/gIB (§2.3, §11).
- [observed] A4X Max joins 18 instances and 72 GPUs through NVLink; RoCE serves inter-subblock traffic (GB300 addendum).

## 4. Portable bench techniques (inferred applications, not attributed procedures)

1. Document expected topology and tray-to-host NIC/port/rail paths before testing; compare this map with observed link inventory. This applies general Clos/routing concepts; it is not a Dutt-prescribed GB300 mapping procedure. [inference] [O’Reilly Ch. 2](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/cloud-native-data/9781492045595/ch02.html)
2. Separate end-host workload evidence from switch/fabric observations. NCCL/perftest measures end-to-end behavior; switch telemetry is needed to support claims about queues, paths or fabric counters. [inference] [NCCL troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)
3. Record the actual device/port, link state/rate, direction, software versions and command line with each measurement so configured intent is not mistaken for measured goodput. [inference] [perftest](https://github.com/linux-rdma/perftest)
4. In the two-hour window, prioritize per-rail directional checks, counter deltas and representative full-rack collectives; disclose skipped pairs and unavailable switch observations rather than implying exhaustive coverage. [inference] [NCCL troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html) [scope](../books.md)

## 5. Canon verdict

**KEEP selectively** as architecture background for Clos, routing and data-center network operations. ## 3. Relevance to rack-bench diagnosis

[inference] The potential overlap is general Linux host/network administration: establish a known host environment; reason about basic networking and routes; manage node reachability; monitor system resources; understand QoS conceptually. Chapter 8's indexed QoS/routing coverage may inform topology and traffic-prioritization background; Chapter 5's monitoring focus may support host-side checks. These are relevance judgments from TOC metadata, not claims that the text teaches modern fabric diagnosis. [Packt Chapter 8](https://www.packtpub.com/en-us/product/mastering-linux-network-administration-9781784399597/chapter/8-understanding-advanced-networking-concepts-8/section/routing-tcpip-traffic-ch08lvl1sec61) [Packt Chapter 5](https://www.packtpub.com/en-in/product/mastering-linux-network-administration-9781784399597/chapter/5-monitoring-system-resources-5/section/maintaining-log-size-with-logrotate-ch05lvl1sec41)

Current NCCL troubleshooting documents RDMA tests, link state and RoCE/IB diagnostics; use them and exact vendor/firmware manuals for the actual test. ## 4. Portable techniques (3–5)

1. [inference] **Verify host identity and baseline before blaming the fabric.** Record OS/kernel, NIC/device and interface/port mapping, addresses, link state and selected route for each test host. This is portable administration practice, not a claim that the book prescribes this exact checklist; NCCL troubleshooting also checks RDMA device/link status. [Packt Ch. 1–2 TOC](https://www.packtpub.com/en-TW/product/mastering-linux-network-administration-9781784399597/chapter/preface-pref/section/what-this-book-covers-preflvl1sec02) [NCCL troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)

[inference] **Inspect routing and topology as distinct from throughput.** Confirm host routes/interfaces and intended peer path; host route inspection cannot prove switch forwarding, adaptive routing or rail use. Chapter 8 TOC supports only general routing/QoS relevance. [Packt Ch. 8 TOC](https://www.packtpub.com/en-us/product/mastering-linux-network-administration-9781784399597/chapter/8-understanding-advanced-networking-concepts-8/section/routing-tcpip-traffic-ch08lvl1sec61) [NCCL troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)
3. [inference] **Separate host-resource bottlenecks from network bottlenecks.** Correlate host CPU/memory/resource pressure during a representative test with per-rail RDMA and NCCL goodput; the book's monitoring chapter is conceptual support only. Do not equate link line rate with achieved collective bandwidth. [Packt Ch. 5 TOC](https://www.packtpub.com/en-in/product/mastering-linux-network-administration-9781784399597/chapter/5-monitoring-system-resources-5/section/maintaining-log-size-with-logrotate-ch05lvl1sec41) [NCCL tests](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests)
4. [inference] **Keep reachability/security checks separate from data-plane pass criteria.** SSH access and service/firewall configuration can explain management or bootstrap failures, but successful SSH does not establish RDMA health; test actual verbs and NCCL paths. [O'Reilly Ch. 3 TOC](https://learning.oreilly.com/library/view/mastering-linux-network/9781784399597/ch03.html) [NCCL troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)
5. [inference] **Treat historical commands as examples, not certification instructions.** This 2015 book predates GB300, modern NCCL and contemporary RDMA stacks. Confirm command availability and semantics against deployed distro/tool versions; prefer current `ip`/`ss` and version-matched RDMA/NCCL documentation to blindly copying legacy `ifconfig`, `route`, `netstat`, distro service or firewall workflows. This is a version-safety warning, not a claim that each named command appears in the book. 1. [inference] **Record interface/link events and host-device state** before and after the run: `ip -s -d link show`, `ip monitor link` captured during the run, and `ethtool <interface>` where supported. This tests kernel IP routing only; it says nothing about RDMA path selection, switch topology, or fabric adaptive routing. [ip-route](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ip-route.8.html)
3. [inference] **Check host receive/softirq pressure as a confound** using `mpstat -P ALL 1` and deltas from `/proc/net/softnet_stat` around a representative TCP/bootstrap test; note CPU/IRQ affinity and NUMA placement if available. The proc format is kernel-version-sensitive: use a version-matched decoder, preserve raw samples, and do not treat fields as universally named or equivalent to NIC/RDMA drops. [proc(5)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/proc.5.html) [mpstat(1)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/mpstat.1.html)
4. [inference] **Use a short TCP baseline only when bootstrap/control transport is relevant:** matched `iperf3` endpoints on a known path, record TCP retransmissions/socket statistics and repeat alongside the same-time NCCL sample. [inference] **Attribute verdict to measured data-plane evidence:** bind `ib_write_bw`, `ib_read_bw`, and latency checks to each HCA/port and direction; compare actual per-rail goodput with the explicitly stated line-rate denominator, inspect RDMA/NIC/switch error and retry deltas, and run NCCL collectives with logs confirming the selected transport/rails. # N07 source supplement: *Linux Networking Cookbook*

Research date: 2026-10-11. All claims below carry a source URL.

## 1. Identity and access

[observed] The supplied O’Reilly Learning link identifies ISBN 9780596102487; its fetch returned HTTP 403, so subscriber chapter access was unavailable in this session. [O’Reilly catalog](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/linux-networking-cookbook/9780596102487). A publicly accessible 634-page PDF copy reproduces the title page, copyright, ISBN and printing history: first edition, November 2007; its copyright page says ©2008. This identifies the first edition, not a distinct 2007 edition. [Public PDF, title/copyright pages](https://www.lions-wing.net/lessons/networking-1/schroder_-_linux_networking_cookbook_oreilly_2008.pdf). The catalog describes a Linux network-administrator recipe book for gateways, monitoring and troubleshooting. Access level: catalog metadata publicly searchable; supplied O’Reilly page denied; TOC/preface accessible in the public PDF mirror (not publisher-hosted); full chapter text not independently reviewed here. [O’Reilly catalog](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/linux-networking-cookbook/9780596102487) [public PDF](https://www.lions-wing.net/lessons/networking-1/schroder_-_linux_networking_cookbook_oreilly_2008.pdf).

## 2. Verified chapters (first-edition TOC)

[observed] Chapter 13, “Network Monitoring with Nagios” (p. 371), and Chapter 14, “Network Monitoring with MRTG” (p. 408), cover service/host checks and SNMP monitoring. Chapter 19, “Troubleshooting Networks” (p. 515), includes ping (19.2), fping/Nmap (19.3), arping duplicate-IP checks (19.4), HTTP throughput/latency (19.5), traceroute/tcptraceroute/mtr (19.6), tcpdump (19.7–19.8), iperf throughput/jitter/loss (19.9), ntop (19.11), and DNS/server troubleshooting. These headings are verified against the first-edition TOC, not inferred from another edition. [Public PDF, TOC pp. v–xiv](https://www.lions-wing.net/lessons/networking-1/schroder_-_linux_networking_cookbook_oreilly_2008.pdf). The preface frames the utilities as quick troubleshooting tools and points to Chapters 13–14 for ongoing monitoring. [Public PDF, Preface pp. xvi–xx](https://www.lions-wing.net/lessons/networking-1/schroder_-_linux_networking_cookbook_oreilly_2008.pdf).

## 3. Relevance to this bench

[inference] This is a useful host-diagnosis supplement, not an RDMA-fabric authority: its 2007 first-edition context predates GB300/NVL72, contemporary NCCL paths, and modern RoCE congestion tooling. TCP/IP reachability, packet capture, and generic iperf throughput do not establish RDMA verbs performance, per-rail health, NCCL transport selection, SHARP use, or correct ECN/PFC operation. Keep this boundary explicit. Modern NCCL guidance instead calls for checking links, low-level RDMA tests, counters, and RoCE NIC/switch congestion signals. [NCCL Networking Troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html).

## 4. Portable bench checks (3–5)

[inference] Keep these as short, read-only host-side triage checks before/after the measured run; record timestamp, host/tray, interface and tool version. They are diagnostic clues, not PASS criteria by themselves.
   1. **Link inventory and state:** `ip -br link` plus platform-available `ibstat`/`ibstatus`; compare expected rail-to-HCA/port mapping, active state and negotiated rate. A host link-up does not prove fabric topology or end-to-end health. [inference] [NCCL troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html).
   2. [inference] **Address/neighbor conflict check:** `ip -br addr`, `ip route`, and targeted `arping` for configured peer addresses where applicable; investigate duplicate-IP or unexpected route/neighbor evidence. This is ordinary host/IP diagnosis, not an RDMA test. [observed] Chapter 19.4 is explicitly “Finding Duplicate IP Addresses with arping.” [Public PDF TOC](https://www.lions-wing.net/lessons/networking-1/schroder_-_linux_networking_cookbook_oreilly_2008.pdf).
   3. **Error-counter deltas:** sample available NIC/RDMA counters before and after controlled load, retaining exact names and values; flag newly increasing errors/retries/drops rather than old nonzero totals. Counter interfaces and semantics are driver/platform-specific; no universal command is promised. [inference] [NCCL troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html).
   4. **Targeted RDMA pair sanity:** use version-matched `ib_write_bw`, `ib_read_bw`, and latency test between selected endpoints, explicitly binding each intended rail and direction; compare measured goodput with the documented per-port line-rate denominator and retain the command/output. This is more relevant than generic iperf, but still does not prove full-rack collective performance. [inference] [NCCL low-level tests](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html) [perftest](https://github.com/linux-rdma/perftest).
   5. [inference] **Capture narrow host evidence:** brief, scoped `tcpdump` only for management/bootstrap traffic or a specifically authorized investigation; avoid treating lack of captured packets as proof of clean RDMA data plane. The book’s tcpdump chapter is generic network troubleshooting. [observed] Chapter 19.7–19.8 TOC headings; limitations for this bench are inference. [Public PDF](https://www.lions-wing.net/lessons/networking-1/schroder_-_linux_networking_cookbook_oreilly_2008.pdf).

## 5. Canon verdict and spine recommendation

**KEEP as an optional, clearly dated host-diagnosis supplement; do not promote to core N07 canon.** [inference] Its most useful additions are simple IP/link triage and the diagnostic mindset of measuring throughput/latency and inspecting traffic. Its generic TCP/iperf and monitoring recipes cannot certify per-rail RDMA, 8 B–16 GB NCCL collectives, rail/topology use, ECN/PFC behavior, flaps, SHARP, or rack-scale PASS. In the existing [books.md](../books.md) spine, add one sentence under the book/canon discussion: “Schroder, *Linux Networking Cookbook*, 1e (2007/2008; ISBN 9780596102487), optional host-side troubleshooting supplement (TOC-confirmed chs. 13–14, 19); dated TCP/IP recipes, not RDMA/NCCL/PFC evidence.” Keep Gregg/Jain/Kurose and the modern NCCL/vendor manuals in their current roles; do not replace or reorder them on this evidence.

## Gaps

- [observed] The O’Reilly fetch denies access. No publisher chapter text supports this review. [Catalog](https://learning.oreilly.com/library/view/-/9780596102487/?orm_source=mcp)
- [observed] The PDF mirror supplies matching ISBN and edition pages. Its publisher authorization remains unknown. [PDF](https://www.lions-wing.net/lessons/networking-1/schroder_-_linux_networking_cookbook_oreilly_2008.pdf)
- [inference] The proposed checks need target-rack validation. They do not establish fabric PASS. [NCCL guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)

None of the retrieved course descriptions or samples establishes coverage of NCCL collectives, per-rail RDMA read/write/latency, line-rate goodput normalization, IB/RoCE topology, ECN/PFC, fabric counter interpretation, flaps, or SHARP. Absence from the accessible outline is not proof those topics never appear in inaccessible video, but there is no basis to cite it for them. [observed] [O'Reilly listing](https://www.oreilly.com/videos/linux-networking/9780138358051) [Coursera course 1](https://www.coursera.org/learn/pearson-linux-networking-basics-and-beyond-video-course-1-ly37x) [Prowse course catalog](https://prowse.tech/recorded_training)

That mapping is an inference from the described course topics, not a claim that any exact command was demonstrated in the video. It cannot support a measured PASS: PASS must come from the rack’s measured NCCL/RDMA/goodput and relevant rail/topology/congestion evidence, as the existing canon explains. [inference] [course 1](https://www.coursera.org/learn/pearson-linux-networking-basics-and-beyond-video-course-1-ly37x) [current books canon](../books.md) [NCCL networking troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)

## 4. Portable host-check techniques (inferred mappings)

These are practical host-side checks suggested by the accessible topic descriptions; they are not asserted as watched lessons, nor substitutes for fabric validation.

1. **Inspect interface/address state:** use `ip -br link` and `ip -br address` to confirm expected interfaces are present, administratively up, and have the intended addresses. Compare against the host/rail inventory. This can catch bootstrap misconfiguration, not prove link quality or RDMA performance. [inference] [course 2 description](https://www.coursera.org/learn/pearson-linux-networking-basics-and-beyond-video-course-2-netjv) [NCCL guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)
2. **Check host routing:** `ip route` (and `ip route get <peer-address>`) verifies the kernel’s selected route/interface for a peer address; capture both directions where relevant. This verifies host routing choice, not switch topology, adaptive routing, rail striping, or path symmetry. [inference] [course 2 description](https://www.coursera.org/learn/pearson-linux-networking-basics-and-beyond-video-course-2-netjv)
3. **Check name/service configuration only when bootstrap depends on it:** verify resolver/host naming and DHCP/static configuration, using the site’s approved read-only tools/configuration. Such checks can explain failed discovery or connection setup; they do not test collective data-plane goodput. [inference] [course 1](https://www.coursera.org/learn/pearson-linux-networking-basics-and-beyond-video-course-1-ly37x) [course 3](https://www.coursera.org/learn/pearson-linux-networking-basics-and-beyond-video-course-3-t2fn4)
4. **Use a basic peer reachability probe as triage:** `ping` a known peer on the intended network and record interface/source selection where possible. A successful ICMP probe does not demonstrate RDMA availability, absence of congestion, or line-rate performance; a failed probe may reflect policy/filtering rather than a failed fabric. [inference] [course 1](https://www.coursera.org/learn/pearson-linux-networking-basics-and-beyond-video-course-1-ly37x) [NCCL guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html)
5. **Compare configuration with actual host state:** use the documented distro manager (`NetworkManager`/`nmcli` or Netplan as applicable) to inspect intended configuration against live addresses/routes; avoid changing configuration during certification without authorization. The course page lists these as sample topics. [observed] [Prowse course catalog](https://prowse.tech/recorded_training) [inference] [course 3](https://www.coursera.org/learn/pearson-linux-networking-basics-and-beyond-video-course-3-t2fn4)

## 5. Canon disposition

**SKIM** the relevant host setup/address/route/service portions if operators need Linux bootstrap triage. **SKIP** as required or core reading for the two-hour rack certification: it is not evidenced as covering the measured NCCL collectives, rail-by-rail IB write/read/latency, goodput versus line rate, topology/routing validation, ECN/PFC, flaps, or SHARP. Keep the existing NCCL, perftest, fabric-vendor, and counter references in `books.md` as the authoritative diagnostic canon. [inference] [current books canon](../books.md) [NCCL guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting/networking_troubleshooting.html) [perftest](https://github.com/linux-rdma/perftest)

## 4. Conditional portable techniques

These are **inferences from the public agenda**, not claims about what was delivered. They do not replace rack measurements or alter PASS criteria.

1. [inference] **Half-split to localize failure:** On a failed collective or perftest, partition implicated hosts/rails or path scope and compare subsets, preserving test conditions; recurse only where topology and binding make the comparison meaningful. 3. [inference] **Separate correlation from cause:** Align timestamps for goodput, rail error/retry deltas, congestion counters, and fabric events; use controlled comparisons before attributing regression to a flap, ECN/PFC, or rail. [O’Reilly agenda](https://learning.oreilly.com/live-events/-/0790145043580/?orm_source=mcp) [canon](../books.md)
4. [inference] **Do not let resilience mask a bad rail:** Where safe and supported, compare alternate paths, but inspect rail-specific evidence; aggregate collective goodput can hide degraded redundancy. [O’Reilly agenda](https://learning.oreilly.com/live-events/-/0790145043580/?orm_source=mcp) [canon](../books.md)
5. [inference] **Keep hypotheses evidence-bound:** If using an LLM during triage, provide sanitized measurements/logs and verify suggestions against local tool help and current vendor docs; do not let generated advice change a measured PASS. [O’Reilly agenda](https://learning.oreilly.com/live-events/-/0790145043580/?orm_source=mcp) [canon](../books.md)

## 5. Canon verdict

**SKIM [inference]:** The agenda supports method background on half-split diagnosis, models, resilience, and causation. It adds no established fabric-specific rules to the NCCL/perftest, rail, topology, ECN/PFC, or goodput canon. No course content is attributed beyond the public agenda, and no source establishes measured target-rack PASS. # TCP/IP Illustrated: ISBN resolution and rack-bench supplement N09

Research date: 2026-10-11. All claims below carry a source URL.

## 1. Identity and access

1. **[observed]** The supplied O'Reilly URL was fetched first and returned HTTP 403, so its catalog metadata/page text could not be inspected. [O'Reilly supplied catalog URL](https://learning.oreilly.com/library/view/-/020163354X/?orm_source=mcp)
2. **[observed]** The publisher's public page identifies *TCP/IP Illustrated, Volume 2: The Implementation*, by Gary R. Wright and W. Richard Stevens, ISBN-13 978-0-201-63354-2. The page's TOC ends with ISBN-10 0-201-63354-X; the preface is signed by Wright and Stevens and dated November 1994. [InformIT publisher page, TOC and preface](https://www.informit.com/store/tcp-ip-illustrated-volume-2-implementation-9780201633542)
3. **[calculated]** ISBN-13 978-0-201-63354-2 is the standard conversion of ISBN-10 0-201-63354-X. [InformIT publisher page, ISBN-13 and ISBN-10](https://www.informit.com/store/tcp-ip-illustrated-volume-2-implementation-9780201633542)
4. **[observed]** The supplied catalog description lists 1995 and 1200pp. The publisher page confirms the exact volume identity; the book preface is dated November 1994 and the scanned front matter carries copyright © 1995. The external scan extracts as 1194 pages, but pagination formats differ, so that extraction does not establish whether “1200pp” is rounded or conflicting. [InformIT publisher page](https://www.informit.com/store/tcp-ip-illustrated-volume-2-implementation-9780201633542); [full-text scan, front matter](https://elhacker.info/manuales/Redes/tcp_ip-illustrated-vol-2.pdf)

## 2. Verified edition and chapter evidence

- **[observed]** The publisher TOC identifies Volume 2, *The Implementation*, and lists Chapters 1–32 plus appendices. Its preface says the text presents the 4.4BSD-Lite TCP/IP implementation, approximately 15,000 lines of C, and assumes basic TCP/IP knowledge, referring readers to Volume 1 for protocol fundamentals. [InformIT publisher page, TOC and preface](https://www.informit.com/store/tcp-ip-illustrated-volume-2-implementation-9780201633542)
- **[observed]** Relevant TOC entries include Chapter 3, “Interface Layer”; Chapters 18–20, “Radix Tree Routing Tables,” “Routing Requests and Routing Messages,” and “Routing Sockets”; Chapter 21, “ARP: Address Resolution Protocol”; and Chapter 31, “BPF: BSD Packet Filter.” [InformIT publisher page, TOC](https://www.informit.com/store/tcp-ip-illustrated-volume-2-implementation-9780201633542)
- **[observed]** Other TOC entries include Chapters 4–5 on Ethernet, SLIP, and loopback; Chapter 6 on IP addressing; Chapters 23–30 on UDP/TCP implementation; and Chapters 12–14 on IP multicast, IGMP, and multicast routing. These are the book's subjects, not modern NCCL collective or SHARP guidance. [InformIT publisher page, TOC](https://www.informit.com/store/tcp-ip-illustrated-volume-2-implementation-9780201633542)

## 3. Relevance to N09 / 18-tray east-west certification

- **[observed]** This is an implementation study of Berkeley 4.4BSD-Lite networking. Its preface explicitly names that codebase; it does not present itself as Linux networking, RDMA verbs, NCCL, GB300/NVL72 topology, RoCE ECN/PFC, or SHARP documentation. [InformIT publisher page, preface](https://www.informit.com/store/tcp-ip-illustrated-volume-2-implementation-9780201633542)
- **[inference]** For the two-hour bench window, its narrow use is conceptual host/bootstrap triage when IP addressing, interface state, neighbor resolution, route choice, or packet visibility blocks test startup/control traffic. It cannot validate RDMA data-path health or establish measured NCCL goodput/line rate. [Canon](../books.md)
- **[observed]** The existing network-research canon explicitly does not rank TCP/IP Illustrated as a core RDMA guide and warns against using TCP implementation material as NCCL payload-path evidence. [Local canon: `books.md`](../books.md)

## 4. Portable host/bootstrap checks (3–5)

These are candidate, read-only checks for host/bootstrap triage, not certification pass criteria.

1. **[inference] Interface/link inventory:** record interface name, administrative/operational state, address, MTU, and mapping to intended host/rail. A mismatch or down host interface can block bootstrap; it says nothing about switch-path or RDMA health. [Linux `ip-link(8)`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ip-link.8.html)
2. **[inference] Address/route sanity:** inspect addresses and route selection to the intended peer/control endpoint; confirm expected source interface/address. This is host IP routing evidence only, not proof of fabric topology or RDMA rail selection. [Linux `ip-route(8)`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ip-route.8.html)
3. **[inference] Neighbor resolution:** inspect ARP/neighbor state for the peer on Ethernet-based bootstrap networks; unresolved/incomplete entries can explain IP reachability failure. Do not apply ARP assumptions to native InfiniBand data paths. [Linux `ip-neighbour(8)`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ip-neighbour.8.html)
4. **[inference] Name/service bootstrap:** resolve peer names and verify the expected management/bootstrap endpoint and port with locally approved tools; record resolved addresses and endpoint. A successful TCP connection proves only that control endpoint, not NCCL/RDMA payload transport. [Linux `getent(1)`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/getent.1.html)
5. **[inference] Packet-level spot check, if authorized:** use a bounded capture on the relevant host interface to check expected bootstrap packets/errors. Absence is inconclusive with wrong interface, permissions, offload, or capture loss; capture cannot certify the fabric. [tcpdump manual](https://www.tcpdump.org/manpages/tcpdump.1.html)

**[inference] Limits and pass rule.** Keep these checks separate from per-rail `ib_write_bw`/`ib_read_bw`, NCCL 8 B–16 GB collectives, transport/plugin logs, counter deltas, topology/routing, ECN/PFC, and SHARP evidence. A host/bootstrap check can identify a blocker but cannot PASS a rack. PASS only on measured workload and per-rail evidence against explicit line-rate normalization and acceptance thresholds; unavailable telemetry is a stated limitation, never a pass. [Canon](../books.md)

## 5. Canon verdict

**[observed]** The preface describes the book as a tutorial on information-collection tools and techniques, chiefly freely available Unix tools, mostly Ethernet/TCP/IP. **[inference]** The inspected scope does not establish modern RDMA/NCCL diagnostic guidance. ## 3. Relevance to the Chennai east-west bench

**[inference]** Its durable contribution is a diagnostic sequence—establish baseline, check connectivity and path, collect packet/device/performance evidence, then combine tools—rather than any current accelerator-fabric procedure. The preface explicitly emphasizes proactive knowledge of normal behavior and information collection; ch. 12 provides troubleshooting strategy. This maps usefully onto an 18-tray, two-hour GB300 NVL72-class bench as a discipline: take before/after evidence, isolate the failing layer, and keep the outcome measured. It does not establish a PASS threshold or substitute for measurements.

**[inference]** For the actual target, prioritize current, domain-specific evidence: NCCL logs and `nccl-tests` for collective goodput, `perftest` for RDMA link/path tests, and deployed vendor/fabric telemetry for rail topology, ECN/PFC and flaps. Compare measured goodput with line rate explicitly; collect counters as deltas and correlate with link/port events. Those are implementation recommendations inferred from the target and modern sources, not techniques asserted by Sloan. ## 4. Portable diagnosis techniques (adaptations, not RDMA instrumentation)

1. **[observed]** The preface advocates knowing normal network behavior and proactive information collection. **[inference]** Baseline before fault-finding: record normal configuration and behavior, then compare the loaded run. **[inference]** Adaptation: save per-rail link state/counters and NCCL/perftest results before and after the two-hour run. Sloan’s proactive-baseline principle is explicit; choosing rail counters and the run window is our inference. [Book scan, ch. 1](http://www.nylxs.com/docs/networktroubleshootingtools.pdf)
2. **[observed]** Chs. 3–4 cover connectivity testing and path characteristics. **[inference]** Use a layered connectivity ladder: separate local link, peer, path and application/collective checks. **[inference]** Adaptation: use ping/route checks only as preliminary reachability evidence, then RDMA tests and NCCL. TCP/IP-era probes do not prove verbs or GPU data-path health. [Book scan, chs. 3–4](http://www.nylxs.com/docs/networktroubleshootingtools.pdf) · [NCCL troubleshooting](https://docs.nvidia.com/deeplearning/nccl/archives/nccl_2312/user-guide/docs/troubleshooting.html)
3. **[observed]** Ch. 5 covers packet capture. **[inference]** Capture and correlate selectively to investigate a suspected protocol/path issue. **[inference]** Adaptation: ordinary TCP/Ethernet captures are not the first-line visibility for RDMA payloads; use them only where the deployed transport and capture point make them meaningful. Prefer NIC/switch counters and fabric tools for ECN/PFC and port events. 4. **[observed]** Chs. 4 and 8 cover path characteristics and performance measurement. **[inference]** Measure at multiple scopes and distinguish capacity from achieved throughput. **[inference]** Adaptation: report per-rail/link measurements and collective goodput separately; compare both against line-rate expectations and note test size/topology. 5. **[inference] Combine independent clues; localize before changing.** Use the path/device view alongside host and application evidence; avoid attributing every throughput symptom to the network. Adaptation: correlate NCCL rank/rail behavior with link flaps, error counters, ECN/PFC telemetry and matched RDMA tests before declaring PASS/FAIL. This is a synthesis for this bench, not a ready-made Sloan recipe.
